speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to lay on the table of the House a copy of the Order in Council which was passed on the 9th day of March, 1915, restricting the transfer of British ships. I do this in accordance with a request of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, made yesterday.
By an Order in Council, dated 23rd January, 1915, the exportation from Canada of vessels, craft and boats of all kinds to non-British destinations is prohibited. This Order in Council, of course, applies only to British ships actually in Canadian ports.
The Order in Council, dated 9th March, 1915, is based on the Bill which is at present under consideration by the imperial authorities, and is intended to apply the restriction to all ships registered in Canada, without regard to where the ship itself may be at the time of the contemplated transfer.
In practice we require a satisfactory guarantee, and bond if necessary, from the intending purchaser that during the continuance of the war the ship will not be used directly or indirectly for the benefit of the enemies of Great Britain.
The Bill now before the imperial authorities does not apply to the Dominion of Canada, hence the necessity for the Order in Council under the provisions of the War Measures Act 67
Mr. LANCASTER presented the eighth report of the select standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines.
I observe that by the report, Bill No. 3, to amend the Railway Act, is withdrawn. Which Bill is that?

It is a Bill standing in the name of the hon. member for East Larnbton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), which deals with two subjects, the question of discrimination under the Act, and the rates charged for the carriage of goods on inland waters.
Bill No. 14 is also withdrawn. What is that Bill?

It is a Bill to confirm an agreement between the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The agreement, however, is not completed. The Bill was not discussed in the committee because the promoters said they were not able to proceed with it, and asked leave to withdraw it.

Hon. J. D. HAZEN presented the report of the commission appointed by Order in Council of the 17th of March, 1913, to investigate and report to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries upon the water levels of the St. Lawrence river at and below Montreal, together with a summary prepared by the chief hydrographer of the survey, showing the results of the investigation; and moved that the report and the summary be printed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member proposes to make a motion for the suspension of the rules in connection with the printing of these documents. It seems to me that the rule, which requires that all matters presented to the House should go directly to the Printing Committee for their consideration, is being more honoured in the breach than in the observance, and if that committee is to be of any value, it seems desirable that it should be allowed to exercise its judgment on many matters before these matters are finally dealt with by a suspension of the rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In view of what you say, I would withdraw my motion and allow the report to go through the ordinary course.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege.



I see in the Montreal Gazette of this morning the following:
At an early hour this morning in the midst of a lengthy speech on the war budget, Mr. i). A. Lafortune, M.P., of Montreal, startled the House of Commons by propounding the following doctrine: " We in Canada should, instead of voting millions to aid England, take the necessary means to cause the disabilities under which French-Canadians suffer in the province of Ontario to disappear."
Mr. Lafortune repeated his statement twice, though questioned iby Mr. Rochon, M.P., as to what power the Federal Government had to interfere.
I declare, Mr. Speaker, that I never said such a thing. The gentleman representing the Montreal Gazette appears to have deliberately put into my mouth words that 1 never used; but I am sure he will do me the justice of correcting his statement. What I said was that the school question was a very important one, and I say now that it is a very important question, but I never meant to say that it was more important than the war; quite the contrary. I hope the gentleman who represents the Montreal Gazette will do me the justice of acknowledging in the next issue of his paper that he made a mistake.
Consideration of the proposed motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment of Sir Wilfrid Laurier thereto, resumed from March 15.

Up to $10 no tax whatever is paid. A man buying a berth costing from $10 up to $30 pays at the rate of one dollar; from $30 to $60 he pays at the rate of $3 and above $60 at the rate of $5. The man pays the higher rate who is able to pay for the better accommodation on the steamer; the wealthier man pays the higher tax just as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance intended that he should. Under these circumstances, the attempt of my right hon. friend to suggest that the poor man is discriminated against by these tariff proposals is not only unworthy of him and of the position he holds, but is absolutely unsupported by any foundation in fact.
My right hon. friend finds protection in the tariff changes. His attitude in regard to free trade and protection has sometimes inspired the country with astonishment. I remember very well in the session of 1902 that his then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir Richard Cartwright, stood up and openly castigated him in the House of Commons because he had fallen away from the doctrine of free trade which he had preached in Opposition; and any one who desires to verify my words need only refer to the speech of Sir Richard Cartwright in the Hansard of that year. My right hon. friend is virtuously indignant about the protected and privileged classes of this country. Does he deny that he maintained the protective principle from 1896 to 1911? Does he deny that in 1907 he and his ministers deliberately increased protection by the tariff then brought down? When I sat where my right hon. friend sits to-day 1 heard them put forward arguments founded on protection in support of the tariff proposals which they had brought down. My right hon. friend in opposition seems to be a most excellent free-trader, at least in theory; but when he comes into power, he seems to be a fairly good protectionist, at least in practice. I remember seeing an anecdote not long ago of an inexperienced drill-sergeant in Great Britain, who was endeavouring to instruct his men in certain physical exercises, and his intention was to	admonish them first to hop
on one	foot and then to hop on
the other, and to keep that up alternately; but, being somewhat inexperienced and getting a little confused in his language, he said: "When I give the word of com-

mand, you must hop first on the right foot and then on the left foot, and keep that up to all eternity." My right hon. friend seems to have a free trade foot and a protectionist foot. When in opposition, he hops on the free trade foot, and when he comes into power, he hops on the protectionist foot. I presume that, so long as my right hon. friend continues in public life, that movement which has been kept up so continuously in. the past may be expected to continue in the future.
What has been the theory of protection upon which the Liberal-Conservative party has proceeded in this country? It is that our raw material plus our labour is equal to the finished product, and that as we have both we ought to use them. We saw no reason why those available resources of Canada which, by the labour of our own people, could be converted into finished products suitable for the use of our people, should not be so converted by the labour of our own people in this country. We stand for that. I have stood for it in the West of Canada as well as in the East, and I have stood for it in power as well as in opposition. With that we have coupled the principle and the belief that we are bound to maintain our customs tariff in Canada on such a standard that labouring men in Canada shall have a fair and reasonable living wage, and that the day shall not dawn that will bring down their standard of living to the scale which prevails in certain other countries which I need not mention.- We want a strong and virile labouring population in Canada to whom a reasonable living wage shall be paid, and we believe it is a good policy for this country that our raw material in Canada, so kept within our own boundaries, shall be converted by the labour of our own people into those articles which are necessary and convenient for the consumption and use of our own people. We say further, so far as that is concerned, that there is no conflict of interest, as my right hon. friend would endeavour to make it appear, between the labouring interests in Canada and the agricultural interests in Canada, because every labouring man, finding employment at a reasonable living wage in industries built up by such a policy as that, establishes the best of all markets, the home market, for the agricultural producer. That is the policy which Canada adopted in 1879, which Canada has kept up ever since and which Canada will keep up in the future, notwithstanding any

assault that my right hon. friend may make upon it.
My right hon. friend, after delivering himself of certain broadsides against that policy of protection, which he maintained for fifteen years, proceeded to declare that we had made an attack upon the British preference. He alleged that British goods, escaping the dangers of the submarines, would find themselves impaled upon our tariff. If I could anticipate an answer, I would ask my right hon. friend again why he increased the British preferential rate in 1907; but my efforts to obtain any answer on that point have been absolutely in vain, so I will not [DOT] detain the House further with them. The hon. Minister of Finance, by the proposal which he has brought down, has given Great Britain a greater preference in our market than she has ever had before. Not only has he done that, but he has established an absolutely new British preference, which in its scope is nearly three times as great as that which my right hon. friend established in 1897. I will prove that to my right hon. friend in a few moments, so that not even he will gainsay it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: The ground I take is that the British exporter has to pay five per cent more that he had to pay before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think everybody knew that. But I had understood my right hon. friend to say that the British preference was decreased. Does he say that now?
I repeat what I said-that the British goods have to pay now five per cent more than formerly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then he does not say that the preference has been decreased. He admits in effect that it has been increased; and the point he desires to make, as I understand him now, is that the British

manufacturer is handicapped as between himself and the Canadian manufacturer. Is that it?

I am too old
a bird to be caught with this chaff. I repeat- and I am sorry that the right hon. gentleman has not seen it (before-that his policy places a handicap on the British exporter as compared with the former condition of things.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And I too am too old a bird to believe that I can get a more direct answer out of my right hon. friend.
And the right hon. gentleman is not even able to twist it as he wants to do.

speechtext:

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance proposes to meet it in part by borrowing and in part by increased taxation, and I say that every additional dollar that we raise by taxation diminishes pro tanto the amount which we must borrow for war purposes. The additional taxation is imposed for that purpose. My hon. friends on the other side of the House may chop logic about that from now until doomsday, but they cannot alter the facts I have just presented.
Another curious feature in the arguments put forward by my hon. friends opposite is this. They say that the increase in the British preferential rate operates in two ways: in the first place, it handicaps the British manufacturer because it is paid by him, and, in the second place, it oppresses the Canadian consumer because it is paid by him. Now, by which one of these oppressed individuals is it really paid, according to my hon. friends? If it handicaps l|he British manufacturer because it was paid by him, it cannot also oppress the Canadian consumer. Up to the present time I have not heard any reasoned argument on the other side of that question, although many assertions have been made. Perhaps some hon. gentleman who follows me will be good enough to take that question up and make it thoroughly clear to us on this side of the House. Is it really paid by both of them?
That is the old question: does the consumer or the producer pay the duty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difficulty is that my hon. friends do not put it forward as a question. They put it forward as an assertion, and say that it operates in two absolutely inconsistent ways.
This discussion began on the 11th day of February. It has proceeded continuously from the 23rd of February up to the present time, and I believe it has occupied nearly 1,000 single columns of Hansard. My right hon. friend has appealed to the example of Great Britain. May I be permitted to quote an example of Great Britain to him? The Finance Act of 1914, one of the greatest measures ever put through the British House of Commons was practically completed in five days, and the report of the debate took 268 columns of Hansard, or about one-quarter of what my hon. friends have occupied here. The Defence of the Realm Consolidation Act was put through in three days and the debate occupied 29 columns. The Grvemment War Obligations Act was put through in f <ar days,

and the debate occupied 94 column t of Hansard. The National Insurance Act occupied three days and filled 3 columns of Hansard. The Injuries in War Compensation Act occupied four days and the discussion filled 4 columns of Hansard. The Trading with the Enemy Amendment Act occupied five days and filled 183 columns of Hansard. The Royal Marines Act occupied three days and filled one column of Hansard. The Army Estimates to provide money to maintain 3,000,000 men of all ranks were discussed on four different days and the discussion filled 333 columns of Hansard.	And all of these measures to
which	I	have	alluded, some	of
them of the first importance, were put through the British House of Commons between the 17th day of November and the 26th day of November. Yet we have been continuously engaged since the 23rd of February in discussing the extraordinary proposals put forward by my right hon. friend and his followers. I trust that the example which I have given to the right hon. gentleman may prove of some service to him and his friends, and that we shall have in the future greater expedition in regard to public business than we have been able to enjoy in the past.
That is rather hard upon your followers; they have not been silent.

They have talked as
much as we have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon.
friends invite an expression of opinion in that regard, I really think that we have been too complimentary to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I think it would have been far better not to have paid them the compliment of answering some of the extraordinary speeches which they delivered. With the desire to be as courteous as possible, which always animates hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, we have felt in duty bound to get up and pretend at least that something approaching an argument had been put forward on the other side of the House and to reply to it.
Does my right hon. friend mean, pretend to answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I do not
mean that at all.
I beg your pardon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In one aspect, I suppose it is a pretence, because if we had to pretend that there was something to

answer we would also have to pretend that we were answering it.
My right hon. friend has put forward to the House and the country the idea that the proposals of the Minister of Finance were of German conception, and I have endeavoured to show that if Germany were in a position to trade with this country at the present time German statesmen and German manufacturers would have a very different conception of the position. But, since my right hon. friend has invited comparisons of that kind, I may be permitted to tell him that the only proposals put forward in this Parliament which ever received the enthusiastic and whole-hearted support of the German Government and the German people were the propolis that he himself put forward two years ago-and I have the evidence under my hand to show it. Since he has invited consideration of Germany's approbation, I have the evidence under my band, taken from one of the greatest newspapers of Germany, the Hamburger Nach-richten. That great journal on the 5th day of June, 1913, contained the following:
Whatever may be decided upon later, the actual decision of the Canadian Senate means at any rate a heavy moral and material loss for the defence of the Empire, for Mr. Borden's promise has been foolishly enough counted on. His offer made an enormous impression in the whole world. Mr. Churchill pointed out this fact especially in the well-known memorandum of the Admiralty. This impression will now not only be destroyed, but people will everywhere obtain tne conviction that England cannot depend upon such help from her colonies. " By rivals and enemies," says the Morning Post to-day, " the decision will be eagerly welcomed. By friends it will be regarded as ominous. The impression must inevitably be created that the solidarity of the Empire is a myth and that those powers which would like to see the overthrow of British naval supremacy need not be discouraged in their efforts by the thought that their challenge would be met by the united resources of the Mother Country and of everyone of the daughter states."
Hear, heaT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As my right hon. friend has seen fit to pass a challenge as Ho whether our proposals or his own aTe most according to German conception, it is my duty to let him see that his own proposals have elicited a favour and an approbation from German public opinion which these tariff proposals could not possibly secure.
Since this war began I have not up to this time uttered one controversial word except to say that if there was to be a fight it would not be a one-sided fight. My right
hon. friend has chosen this moment to open fire upon us with a vote of want of confidence, and to raise issues of a purely partisan and controversial character. I desire to inform him that we do not shirk from his criticism or from the issues which he raises, conscious as we are that, confronted by the most tremendous responsibilities ever imposed upon the shoulders of Canadian public men, we have striven in the past and will strive in the future to do our duty to this Dominion and to the British Empire.

I did not wish to interrupt my right hon. friend, and I now rise for the purpose of an explanation. My right hon. friend has alluded to a certain interview which took place between him and me previous to the session. He stated that he had given me the programme of what he proposed to do during the session. He told me, according to my recollection, that his intention was to make this a war session, and a war session only. He told me that the measures which he intended to bring down were an appropriation of $100,000,000 and an Act authorizing the issue of Dominion notes by the Government. He told me further that there would probably be some tariff changes. I do not believe that the right hon. gentleman told me anything else. In answer to that, I told him that I was quite satisfied to have a war session, and that if we on this side of the House were to bring down any question outside of a war question, we would give him notice of it. So far as I recollect, that is what took place between my right hon. friend and myself, and nothing else. I speak from memory, hut upon this I believe my memory is right. I am sure I am in the right as to what took place between my right hon. friend and myself, and I have simply this to say to him: Everybody has a sense of honour. To me, confidential conversations are confidential, and are never revealed. If the right hon. gentleman chooses to bring this before the public, I have no objection; I have given my version.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I might say to my right hon. friend that he himself first introduced the subject by stating that he had not been consulted, and I esteemed it my right and my duty to state to what extent he had been consulted. He was consulted .to the extent which I have already stated, and my statement in that regard does not, as I understand, differ materially from his own. I told him that we had a

fiscal measure to introduce, and naturally he knew as well as I that I could not give the details of it to him at that time. Besides that, I gave to him not only our programme, but a copy of every Bill which we had ready and proposed to introduce. To that extent I did consult my right hon. friend, and I am not aware that in stating that I gave him this information I am violating any breach of confidence.

If my right
hon. friend means that we had an interview upon the tariff similar to the consultation that took place in England between Austin Chamberlain and Lloyd George, he is absolutely mistaken.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N. B.):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is not an easy task to attempt to answer the somewhat impassioned speech made by the right hon. leader of the Government, especially after he had travelled so far afield and imported into this discussion matters which to the ordinary man at least would seem to have been better left out. My right hon. friend the leader of the Government has almost found fault with his own side for answering the charges and arguments which have been put forward from this side of the House. Well, then, some of the arguments and some of the charges put forth from this side of the House must have been very potent. Only yesterday the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) was asked to give way to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in order to give that gentleman an opportunity of answering our arguments; and to-day the right hon. leader of the Government has taken the place of two prominent followers who were supposed to speak this afternoon. He has taken the words out of their mouths and jumped into the debate himself. The arguments from this side of the House must certainly be doing something in the country, for they are doing a lot in the mind of my right hon. friend. My right hon. friend has seen fit rather to try to show that the leader of the Opposition has not been playing this game fairly, that he has not been observing the so-called truce. But the only evidence which he put forward was the statement that he went to the right hon. leader of the Opposition and gave him certain information; it is not necessary that I should refer to it at any great length because we have had the statements of both these gentlemen and the House can judge for itself. But my right 
hon. friend the leader of the Government has not met in the least the criticism of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. The leader of the Opposition referred to the condition of affairs that existed in England, where there was a real party truce, where the Opposition was taken into the confidence of the Government, where the chief censor was one of the leaders of the Opposition, and where the Opposition not only knew what was going on in connection with the war, but were given an insight into the financial measures proposed by the Government. If my right hon. friend would do himself the justice of reading what has been said by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, I think he would see that he has placed the matter in a very, very unfair light. And in case my right hon. friend has not read that statement I am going to trouble the House to listen while I read every word that the leader of the Opposition uttered on that subject. He was contrasting the attitude of this Government with the attitude of the British Government, and was trying to bring himself in line with the attitude assumed by the Opposition in Great Britain. The statement is found on page 885 of the Unrevised Hansard. After quoting extensively from the Saturday Review, the leader of the Opposition on that occasion said:
I commend these words to the attention of the House. You will see that in Great Britain the Opposition were consulted by the Government as to their financial proposals. This is a matter of record and of history. I might go further than this newspaper goes and say that at all stages of the war, from the first to the present day, the Opposition have been kept in constant consultation by the powers that be; they were consulted as to military operations, and at every step were asked to give their advice. We were not so consulted. If we had been honoured in the same way- not that I claim anything in that respect, but representing here a great party comprising almost half of the population, having views of their own on many of the financial problems which now confront us, olalming to be as patriotic as the other side, and claiming to have done their duty as amply as was in their power-I say that, if we had been consulted, we should have been happy to give our views as to the policy to be pursued. I do not say that our views would have been accepted; but certainly there would have been an effort on my part at all events to give way on some of my own views, and I might have felt it right to ask the other side to give way on some of their views also, so that we might have been unanimous in policy as we have been unanimous in the objects which policy is to serve. But we were not consulted. I do not complain of this; I have no right to complain. But my hon. friend the Finance Minister has no right to complain either if to-day we have

to take issue with him, and take issue sharply, upon the propositions which he has laid before the House.
The whole point is in that one paragraph from the speech of my right hon. leader. The right hon. leader of the Government has dragged into this discussion the Navy debates; but I am not going to follow him in that, except to say that if the right hon. leader of the Opposition may have any troubled dreams over the Canadian naval question, I do not know what must be, not only the dreams, but the waking thoughts of the right hon. leader of the Government on that question. If my right hon. friend should have any troubled dreams over the naval question I do not know of any one who should be more afflicted, not only with dreams but with waking thoughts, in regard to the naval question than the right hon. leader of the Government, a gentleman who in 1909 subscribed to the only British, Imperial naval policy which was ever brought forward in Canada, a gentleman who in 1910 departed from that policy in order to obtain the votes of the men sitting behind him from the province of Quebec, a gentleman who adopted a policy in 1912 and 1913, which, if it had been adopted by the people of Canada, would have been absolutely futile for the simple reason that it never could have been accomplished and put in operation in time to be of any assistance during this present war. He turned down the policy which he had adopted in 1909, which was adopted by this Parliament in 1910, which was attempted to be carried into effect by my right hon. leader in 1911 and which, if it had been carried into effect, would have accomplished the object for which we intended it; that is, it would have afforded some means of protection to Canada and the rest of the Empire in this hour of need. No wonder my right hon. friend the leader of the Government leaves the chamber when any one commences to discuss naval affairs, I am surprised that he even stays in the chamber and discusses the question himself.
But this is not a question of the navy; it is a question of the Budget that we are discussing and for the few minutes that I purpose addressing the House I intend to confine myself strictly to the Budget and not to discuss the navy question. Any time hon. gentlemen opposite want to raise a naval discussion in this House, or on the stump, or anywhere else, they will not have
very much trouble in finding some one who will give them a Roland for their Oliver.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Government has taken my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to task very severely because he says he has tried to create in the minds of the people a class distinction, that he has tried to place class against class, that he has tried to place the rich man against the poor man. If pointing out to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and to the country at large, that the logical result of the financial proposals which he has brought down means the placing of class against class, the placing of an unfair and unjust burden on the shoulders of the poor man and allowing the rich man to go scot free, we accept the challenge and we are prepared to discuss that in this House or on any platform or hustings and we are prepared to discuss it until the matter is, as it will be, finally settled by the people. After all that is the great issue brought up by the proposals of the Minister of Finance. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) yesterday, I must say, delivered a splendid speech in the House, a speech so different from that of his leader to-day or of the Minister of Finance a few days ago, a speech so different in tone, so different in argument, and on a much higher plane. While I am as sensible of political antagonism as perhaps any other man, yet I would not feel that I was doing my duty if I did not compliment my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon the high tone which he gave to the debate yesterday afternoon.
The good example.

Yes, on the good example that my hon. friend sets the House, and one which I am sorry to say has not been followed by his chief this afternoon. But even the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce belaboured the matter for fifteen minutes in order to show that in England there was no opposition to the Government's financial proposals. In England the Government did not change their financial policy; they went on and raised their money by the same old method. In Canada the Minister of Finance is almost revolutionizing the fiscal conditions wlhich have prevailed in this country during the last fifteen or eighteen years. When they are revolutionizing the fiscal system, and doing that in war time, our hon. friends opposite say:

You are disloyal, you are unpatriotic, you are unBritish, you are not good Canadians, you are not playing the game fairly when you challenge this proposition and challenge it by a vote of this House. I wondered if the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen who have spoken had in view some of the gentlemen who sit behind him and who have themselves dealt with this proposition, I wondered if the hon. member for Ri-mouski (Mr. Boulay) would not rather have got out of this House without voting upon this question, I wondered if some other hon. gentlemen of the same family as the hon. member for Rimouski would not have been very much pleased if this proposal could have been adopted without putting them under the painful necessity of placing themselves on record either for or against it. These are only internal matters affecting my right hon. friend and his friends, but I only thought it wise to throw out the hint to let him understand that we are taking notes of what is going on and that we are listening to such speeches as that which came from the hon. member for Rimouski a few days ago.	.
As I understand these proposals, my Ihon. friend the Finance Minister says that there is, or will be, a great gap between revenue and expenditure for the coming year, and it is the duty of the Minister of Finance to make up that gap-not the whole of it; he does not profess that he is going to completely fill the gap. The Minister of (Finance made half a dozen references to the fact that he had to find a million dollars a day, a burden which 1 admit would even tax the resources of a rich man like my hon. friend the Finance Minister. We have had this statement in his Budget speech and we had it put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday, that even with all these herculean efforts of the 'hon. Minister of Finance, he is only going to raise half of this amount. He says: I am going to have an enormous amount of trouble even to raise half of it, and I am going to have that trouble because of the unfortunate position in which you left me when you handed over this bankrupt estate in 1911. I was very much interested in listening to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance talking about that bankrupt estate. I have just read over what he said, and I am still more interested. My hon. friend used these words, and I will just read them to him lest he forgets. I think there must be a good many things in the two or three hours' address which he
[Mr. Carvell. 1
delivered that my hon. friend would like to forget, and while it may not be kind it is an absolute necessity to recall some of these things to (his attention as I go along. He said:
In estimating the value of an estate, do we not take into consideration liabilities direct and indirect, debts owing, notes in hand, en-dorsations, guarantees given by the decedent who left the estate? Is it a rich legacy, if the legatee with a certain sum of ready money, is left also the obligation of millions of dollars of liabilities? That is the kind of rich legacy that I have inherited as Minister of Finance-some ready money in the treas iry, but obligations, not of millions, not of tens of millions, but literally of hundreds of millions of dollars of direct and indirect liabilities, that I have had to meet since I have become Minister of Finance of this country.
The hon. member then proceeded to enumerate some of these terrible burdens that had been cast upon his shoulders. The only thing which he mentioned in his remarks was that he had been compelled to pay a large sum of money on account of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific seems almost to be something on the brain of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says
" here, here," and it is something that is on the brains of others. There is not a man in this House who does not, down in his heart, admit that the Bill providing for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific was the finest piece of Imperial legislation that was ever passed by the Parliament of Canada and I will tell you why.
