But there can be no doubt that the hon. gentleman finds himself in an unhappy predicament. He has told us-^and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) laboured the point for a long time yesterday afternoon-that this war created the emergent financial condition that faces us in Canada to-day. These hon. gentlemen tell us that on account of the war they are compelled to do those things that they would not otherwise do.
I am not going to repeat the figures given by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) at an earlier stage of this debate, but I will refer to them briefly. The imports are a pretty fair indication of the financial condition of a country because they exemplify the purchasing power of the people. Compare our imports in January before the
war with the January of the previous year. Those imports dropped from $34,000,000 to $26,000,000. In February they were $25,000,000 as against $35,000,000 for the year before. In March the drop was from $45,000,000 to $34,000,000 and in April from $32,000,000 to $23,000,000. In May the imports fell off from $40,000,000 to $28,000,000; in June from $37,000,000 to $27,000,000, and in July from $39,000,000 to $26,000,000. The war conditions had nothing to do with that. Nor was it on account of non-production, because the country was producing as much as ever. Our exports were not decreasing to any great extent, though our imports were decreasing. I will not go into a history of the causes of that condition of affairs because it would take too long. All I say to the Minister of Finance is that he does not treat the country fairly when he tries to convince the people that the unfortunate condition in which he finds himself at the beginning of the war is due to the war. It is due to his own mismanagement and bungling; it is due to the fact that he did not conserve the revenue of the country as he should have done, he did not save his surpluses, he did not provide for a rainy day. As the hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) said, he squandered his money like a drunken sailor; and when the banks began to shut down on western lands, investment and something like a panic came on, he found himself without means to meet the situation. Then came the war, and he had nothing on which to draw in his time of trouble.
Now, we have to face the condition of affairs as it is. There is no doubt there is a serious condition of affairs confronting the minister. The minister says he must devise ways and means to meet it. That is what we say. But, with all the omniscience which he takes to himself, he has not had very much trouble about it. He himself says, and therefore it must be true, that this thing did not bother him at all, because he saw his way through. As I wish to be sure to quote him correctly, I give his words as they are to be found at page 891 of Hansard:
I have always been able to see my way through. I saw my way through in the year 1913, when, in the midst of that great financial stringency brought about by the Balkan war and by the shadow of this great war cast before, 1 was struggling with the consequences of that ruinous railway policy launched by hon. gentlemen opposite. In the midst of this war which is not only the greatest war in the history of the world, but greater, as I said the

other day, than the aggregate of all wars up-to-date, I see my way through, just as 1 saw it through in August last, when the outbreak of this tremendous trouble threatened to overwhelm the finances and the commerce of the world. I saw my way through then. T see my-way through now, and at no time since the outbreak of this war have the prospects been so good, so far as this country is concerned, as they are to-day.
My hon. friend saw a great many visions when this war unfortunately burst upon us on the 4th day of August, 1914. For three years he had been trying to do something for the special interests to which he owed his position in public life. He saw that the people of Canada would never allow him to do what his friends would like him to do, and that the only way in which he could accomplish his end would be to act under some emergent condition. My hon. friend saw that he was not keeping his pledges; he saw that he was not able to do what he had promised to do. When the war came he saw that the way was open to him, and in the August session of Parliament he commenced to increase the duties upon manufactured articles and to place duties upon some goods formerly free. At that time I pointed out that while we were not opposing his proposals, the consequences of his method of taxation would be objectionable. My hon. friend at that time himself foreshadowed tariff changes at the next session of Parliament. He knew exactly what he was going to do; he knew that he was going to impose upon the people of this country a protective tariff worse than has ever been known in Canada, and as bad as any which has ever been imposed in the United States. My hon. friend, therefore, is secure in saying that he "saw through" these things; in the proposals which he has brought down, he is merely carrying out the things which he foresaw last year. He reasoned with himself thus: If I reduce the expenditure of this country to what it ought to be, or to anything like what it was when I assumed office three years ago, I shall not have to impose any more taxes, and I shall not be able to carry out the policies which will please my friends. As a result of this reasoning, therefore, my hon. friend boosted the expenditure. It k true that he brought it 'down a little lower than it was during the previous year, but he asked for an expenditure of $180,000,000 or $190,000,000 to carry on the affairs of the country, entirely aside from the amount required for war expenditure. Any reasonable businessman, any reasonable financier, or even a reasonable politician, would take the other course and proceed to 
reduce expenditure instead of increasing it. In all the arguments which my hon. friend has put forward on this subject, he has never said that he cannot reduce expenditure ; he argues that he cannot stop spending money. He said the other day that if a private individual wanted to close down his business, he could do so. Every one knows that the- business of this country cannot be closed down; the Minister of
5 p.m. Finance cannot do it, and nobody wants him to do it. All we want the minister to do is to be reasonable; to reduce expenditure. If he wants any better evidence than I can give him of the desirability of taking this course, I direct his attention to what was practically an admission on the part of a former Minister of Finance (Sir George Foster) a man who knows something about finances that the ordinary expenditure of this country could be cut down to the extent of $30,000,000 a year. Nothing in the whole speech of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday afternoon, able as it was, so impressed me as that almost straight admission on his part that the Minister of Finance could have reduced the expenditure by $30 000,000. But the minister exp-cts to raise only about $30,000,000. He admits that he is going to have a deficit of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 at the end of the financial year. If he had done what his colleague almost said he could have done, he would have closed up the gap between revenue and expenditure and would have obviated the necessity for special taxation. But if he bad done that he would not have given any protection to the manufacturers. My hon. friend became indignant a few days ago when my honoured leader intimated to him that the net result of this tariff would be increased protection. It is true that my hon. friend said that his indignation was due to the intimation of the right hon. gentleman that that was the object of the tariff increases, but I am going to deal not with what my hon. friend's object was, but with what the results of the proposed legislation will be.
It has been argued by the Finance Minister, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the Prime Minister that in order to get revenue you must tax free goods or raw materials. I admit that there may be times of national stringency when a tax should be imposed on raw materials, but I do not believe that the time has come for taking that course; on the contrary, I believe we are a long way from any such necessity. But hon. gentlemen say that they have to

tax raw materials. The lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce told us yesterday afternoon that last year we imported $208,000,000 worth of free goods. If the same amount be imported this year and taxes of 5 and 7* per cent be paid thereon, the treasury will get between $10,000,000 and $13,000,000. But here is where the fallacy of this argument comes in. Hon. gentlemen say that if you increase the taxes upon the raw materials, you must increase the duty upon the manufactured article. That may be true to some extent, but when you increase the duty upon the manufactured article to the same extent that you increase the duty upon the raw product, the only person you treat fairly is the manufacturer. I do not know exactly what proportion the cost of the raw material would bear to the cost of the manufactured product, but I think I am safe in saying that cost of the raw material would amount to not more than one-third of one-fourth the cost of the finished product. My hon. friend says:	we compel the manufacturer to pay 5 or 7i per cent upon the raw material which he brings into this country; therefore we should allow him a charge from 5 to 7i per cent more for the finished product. Let us take a few examples. Automobiles are now being purchased by people of moderate means as well as by the richer people; the automobile is an article which every man wants who is able to have one. I suppose that the duty upon the raw material entering into the manufacture of an automobile would be about half the duty upon the finished article. The extra duty upon wool would not amount to one-fourth, one-fifth or one-sixth of what it would be on the finished product. The cost of raw cotton would be probably one-half the cost of the finished product. In the case of furniture, the cost of the raw material would be probably one-tenth of the cost of the finished product. And so on; in every case there is a pronounced discrepancy between the cost of the raw material and the cost of the finished product. The illustration which is afforded by boots and shoes probably emphasizes more clearly the point which I am trying to make than that afforded by any other article of commerce produced in Canada.
A tender spot.

Yes, it is. I notice that one witness said yesterday you bad to have tender boots because you had tender feet. I am going to discuss this matter from the cold standpoint of dollars and cents. There 68
is probably no article of consumption in Canada that is so wholly manufactured within our own borders as boots and shoes. The duty, I am sorry to stay, was high enough before; in my judgment it was much higher than it should have been.
I know my friend will say: Your Government are responsible for that. They have some sins to answer for and I am willing they should answer. Now during last year we imported altogether of boots and shoes, as nearly as I can find from the trade returns, $4,349,000 worth of boots and shoes, upon which we paid $1,135,000 in duty and, of course, if on the same quantity of hoots and shoes you added an extra 7i per cent import duty-because the imported shoes all come from the United States-you will find that there would be in the vicinity of $300,000 extra duty. I do not know exactly what would be the factual cost per person for boots, but I have assumed that it would be $5 per person for boots in Canada. I know that' estimate is low enough, and I am of the opinion that the average would be very much more than that, it might go up to $7 or $8 a person; but certainly $5 would be the minimum per capita cost of boots in Canada. If you have 8,000,000 people in Canada, that would mean a total cost for boots and shoes in one year of $40,000,000, 'and if we have imported $4,000,000 or $4,500,000, then that gets you down to $35,000,000 worth of hoots and shoes manufactured in Canada. I do not think my hon. friend can get away from that. As the imported boots and shoes all come from the United States, you have a right to add on the 7 ot 11 per cent -a>s extra cost to the people of Canada because the shoe manufacturers-and I am not finding any fault with the boot and shoe manufacturer, he is just an ordinary human being like the rest of us-being given a Tight to add on just enough additional price to keep out the foreign product, will iadd it on, and as there is enough duty now to keep out the foreign product if you add an additional 7i per cent that will be added to the price, the foreign product will still be kept out.
Is that fair ? Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the price of boots and shoes in this country has gone up in accordance with the tariff ?
Certainly it has.
Certainly it has not.

Certainly it has. There is not a commodity in Canada that has not gone up or will not go up. The hon.



lember talks about things going up. I was in Montreal the other day, and w>anted to buy some new spark plugs for my automobile. I went into a store and they gave me a bill and added on the 7\ per cent on the bill.
That may be.
I want to say from my knowledge of the business-
Did the hon. gentleman not support the late Government which raised the duty on shoes by 5 per cent?

One gets nauseated and tired of this tu quoque argument. I was honest enough, more honest than my hon. friend ever was in discussing a matter in this House, to say that, in my judgment, the duty on boots and shoes was greater than it should be. I said that to-day. I said that last year, I always have said it, and I do not think the Solicitor General is going to cover himself with any great glory by asking foolish questions of that kind. I condemned the former duty on boots-

Only since you got over
there have you condemned it.

If I was unkind enough to return the tu quoque, I should say that the best speech the hon. gentleman ever made in this House was made in pleading for a reduction of duty on agricultural implements; and now the hon. gentleman will stand up and not only vote for this increase of duty, but defend it. I am not employing the tu quoque argument. I do not care what he did when on this side of the House;. I am trying to argue on things as they are to-day. Let me show my hon. friends the real position of things to-day, when this country is at war, when every person ought to be straining every effort to bring this war to a successful conclusion, when the Government of this country have no right to tax the people white in order to satisfy and placate their political friends over the country, but when it ought to be the duty of the Government to try to treat the people fairly, to make the cost of living as low as possible consistent with raising a revenue. Those are the things I am trying to point out, and not what I or my hon. friend may have voted for three or four years ago. The Tory party never seems to realize that this world moves, and that what may have been true 100 years ago may not necessarily be true to-day, that what was true ten years ago may not be true to-day. The mere fact that my hon. friend interrupted my argument shows that

it is absolutely unassailable; and as the Solicitor General is to follow me, I invite him to answer this proposition and to show that the people in this country will not pay five times as mueh to the boot and shoe manufacturing concerns as the Government will get out of the increased duty on boots and shoes and leather and raw products by adding the 5 per cent and 7J per cent duty on boots and shoes and raw materials that enter into them.
And since my hon. friend has interrupted me, I hope he will do me the courtesy and the justice of at least trying to explain away this one point: Have I not pretty effectually answered the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite? I say that if the duty on the finished product is increased by 5 per cent, the duty upon the raw material ought to be increased by 15 per cent; and then the manufacturers would be compelled to pay something into the revenues of this country, and they would not be able to turn around and charge their customers more than they are paying to-day; for if they raised their prices beyond that point the foreign article would come in. For instance, the home manufacturer has his boots and shoes priced just low enough to prevent foreign-made boots and shoes from coming in. If what I have suggested were done, some sort of equilibrium would be created between the raw material and the finished article; and the manufacturer would be compelled to pay something to the Government in the way of revenue, and would not be able to make any extra profit out of the common people in the sale of his articles. And what is true of boots and shoes is true of almost every other article in the whole commerce of Canada. You can take article after article ad infinitum, and you will find exactly the same thing. Therefore I think I am perfectly right when I say that the cost of the manufactured article is at least three times as much as the cost of the raw material, and that, to be logical, you should increase the duty on the raw material by three times the duty on the finished product. My hon. friend might ask: Would you advocate that? No, never. I hope I shall never be guilty of advocating such a policy as that. I would never advocate a policy that would increase the ordinary burdens of the people of this country at a time when they were bending their energies and spending every possible dollar in order to carry this country and this Empire through such terrible conditions as are confronting us to-day.
I would reduce the expenditures of this country and get down to something like 68i
decent, honest Government. I would get rid of the horde of unnecessary officials and of all the little armouries that are being built at country cross roads in Ontario. I would get rid of all these things, and do business on business principles, and then it would not be necessary to increase the duty on the raw material or on the manufactured article. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister threw back at us this afternoon that nobody on this side of the House had made any proposal to get around the difficulty, and the Minister of Finance the other evening said that only one hon. gentleman on this side of the House, the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt), had made even a suggestion how to meet this great gap between revenue and expenditure. I have tried to point out to the Minister of Finance what I would do were I in his place, but the ordinary dictates of business management should have suggested these proposals, without them having to be called to his attention by members on this side of the House. But he does not seem to understand.
1 am going to tell him a few more things that I would do if I were in his place, and it is no use his coming hack with the tu quoque argument: why did you not do it when you were in power? Well, in the first place, when we were in power it was not necessary to do these things. When we were in power there was no great Imperial war on, as there is to-day. There was a war from 1899 to 1902 in which Canada took a part; but the cost was not very great, and there was no increase in the duties, no increase in the burdens of the people. From the day the Liberal party came into power in 1896 down to when they went out of potver in 1911, there was nothing but one long succession of surplus after surplus, and it was not necessary to resort to direct taxation or to those means of raising the revenue which are adopted in countries that find that problem difficult. Not that the tariff under the Liberal party was not high enough, even higher than it ought to have been. I will say that, if it is of any comfort or assistance to my hon. friend the Solicitor General. I say that when the Liberals were in power the tariff on goods coming into this country was as high as it ought to have been, and in many cases much higher; and if my hon. friends wants to point out cases I do not think that he and I will get very far apart. Take wool for instance. I say the tax on wool was exorbitant. Or if he takes boots

and shoes I agree with him. I agree that the duty was higher than it should have been on dozens and dozens of articles which enter into the home of the ordinary working ' man. But, because this party erred, it should not be flung back in my teeth that I am not sincere in the arguments I put fofward. I am not responsible for the tariff as it existed then. What I say is that the tariff as it existed in 1911 was such an improvement on the tariff as it exists to-day, that a man does not have to be an out-and-out free trader in order to show the inconsistencies and unfairness of the present proposals.
I would try my utmost to increase production in this country. I would not try to discourage those who are trying to raise products to the best of their power. I would not put a duty on fertilizers. My hon. friends may say, now you are talking shop, or something narrow. But let me tell my hon. friends that the duty on fertilizers is no small thing to the district I represent. Let me just give some figures. The total importation of fertilizers into the whole of Canada for the last fiscal year was valued at $602,148, and I have here a return from the Commissioner of Customs showing that of that amount, $118,000 was imported into my own town of Woodstock in New Brunswick; that is, about one-fifth of the total importation into Canada went into my home town. I also find that $10,000 went to the town of Debec, only 12 miles away; and I see that St. John and St. Stephen took $50,000 more; so that almost $200,000, or nearly one-third Of the total importation of fertilizers, went to the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that manufactured fertilizers?

Practically all, yes.
Pretty nearly one-third of the total importation went into the province of New Brunswick, and three-fourths of that into my own constituency. In addition to that, enormous quantities are manufactured at home. I know that $400,000 of fertilizer is used in my own constituency, and yet my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is putting a duty on that. He is asking the New Brunswick farmer to produce more than he did last year, and at the same time he is putting a tax upon the very thing which the farmer must have in order to carry on his agricultural operations. Is that logical? But my hon. friend never attempted to be logical id the imposition of this tariff. Logic is the last thing which he had in his mind. He

simply said, I will import from the Manufacturers' Association their tariff expert, and! hand these things over to him. The tariff expert simply puts 7i per cent on everything, whether it goes to the farmer or the rich man, and regardless of whether it is logical or not. Perhaps my hon. friend does not realize that one of the important ingredients in fertilizers is potash, which comes altogether from Germany. The ordinary commercial mixture is what is called a four, six -and ten, that is, four of ammonia, six of phospherus and ten of potash. The very best you can purchase to-day is four, eight, four; that is four of potash instead of ten.
You can only get 4 per cent of potash where you usually get 10 per cent. We are compelled to pay a higher price this year than we were last year. Without this article we cannot successfully carry on our farming operations. While we paid $4 a ton last year, this year we are going to pay nearly $6.50 or $7.50 a ton. The result will be that men will not buy it and they will not be able to carry on their operations as they have done before. I am pointing out to the Minister of Finance the result of this illogical tariff, the result of putting on a tax to get around a little difficulty in order to help his manufacturing friends.

Does my hon. friend know how much of this fertilizer is usually applied
per acre?

Yes, I do, and I will tell you all about it, because it may surprise you to know it, but I am a farmer myself. If you are going to use fertilizer on grain land you will require to use 300, 400 or 500 pounds to the acre; for potatoes you will require to use from 1,500 to 2,000 pounds per acre and if you want a particularly heavy crop you will have to use a little more. For different crops you will have to grade it according to the necessities of the case. The first thing I would do would be to delete that part of the tariff and reduce the cost of fertilizer. I want to do everything I can to induce people to produce two blades of grass where one was produced before, to produce two bushels of oats where one was produced before or to produce two bushels of wheat where one was produced before. I want to see the agricultural people of this country encouraged to produce more than they ever produced before. What this Empire needs is agricultural produce more than anything else I know of. This Empire needs all the food products that it can

possibly raise. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. 'Burrell) is going all over Canada preaching the propaganda of patriotism and production and the notices of the meetings I receive are surmounted by the flag. That is all right, I have no fault to find with that at all. I wish God to speed him and I hope that he may succeed in his campaign to bring about a greater production than we have ever known before. But the Minister of Finance comes along and at one swoop puts one part of the country at least in such a position that it is absolutely impossible to go on and produce anything like the crops that have been produced during the last three or four years.
The next thing I would do is this; I would see that as far as possible these taxes were so adjusted that the rich man would pay his share and not put them on the shoulders of the poor man. These hon. gentlemen will tell you that this is not an ordinary fiscal policy, they will tell you that this is an emergent condition of affairs, that the Empire is at war, and as the Prime Minister said to-day, it is the duty of this Government to keep at war until the war is finished. We agree with that. We tell the Finance Minister that if he wants to have more money than the ordinary revenues of the country will produce it is his duty to place his request before the House and take a vote upon it. We say to him: bring down your vote for $100,000,000 and give us an opportunity of voting for it; we want to help you to carry on this just war and we are anxious to know why you have not brought forward your vote of $100,000,000 because when you do we will vote for it; if $100,000,000 is not enough then make it $150,000,000 and we will vote for it just the same; we are not going to ask you questions as to how you are going to expend it; we will have to trust you to spend it and when we come back later on, or next year, it may be our painful duty to criticise how you spent it as we have now to criticise how the money voted last session has been expended. In the meantime you can go on and spend it. But if the Minister of Finance says that he has to put additional burdens upon the shoulders of the people of this country let him not place those burdens on the backs of those least fit to bear them.
The principal method by which, he proposes to raise these taxes is by tariff taxation. I have discussed that. I have pointed out that while he is going to get some additional revenue-not very much-he will get some additional revenue on raw materials and on manufactured articles-he will find that the revenue will not be as much as he has figured it.
He has resorted to a principle which I commend very heartily and.that is the principle of direct taxation. But here again my hon. friend has entirely exempted his financial and monopolistic friends from the operation of this tax and has put the burden upon the shoulders of poor people. My hon. friend smiles. . This matter was considered so important that his leader this afternoon had to take up an hour in order to answer the -case made by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition two days ago. Let us see what he is doing. He says: I am taxing the banks. I give him credit for that and I have no fault to find with the banks either. He says the Bank of Montreal is going to pay $135,000 a year. The Bank of Montreal is paying to its shareholders $1,500,000 a year in the way of dividends and he is taking $135,000 out of them. The stock of the Bank of Montreal is as high as it ever was before the war. I do not think that it has dropped more than three or four points since the outbreak of the war. The stock of the Royal Bank has only dropped two or three or four points. The stock of all these banking institutions is as valuable as it was before the war. Why? Because the banks are making just as much money as they did before. I am finding no fault with the banks, but when the banks are able to pay 10 per cent, 12 per cent, and in some eases higher dividends, they can afford to make some sacrifices. While I give my hon. friend credit for imposing taxation upon the banks my criticism 13 that the taxation is only half what it ought to have been.
Then he has imposed a tax on the average man, the man who travels on the railway, and we know that such a tax affects the ordinary man much more than it does the rich man. That has all been argued by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. We have heard the attempted answer of the right hon. the Prime Minister. He cannot get away from the fact that he is imposing taxes upon the poor man to a greater extent than on the rich man. Then, coming to the question of express receipts, we all know that the rich man does not get express receipts. Express receipts are only for small amounts of money transmitted by the ordinary, poor man. The express company does not pay the tax. The tax is paid by the people themselves. Then you come to the postal revenue. If the Govern-

ment feel that it is necessary to impose this tax I do not know that I am finding so much fault with it. Probably the wealthy classes will pay their fair share of the burden resulting from the taxation upon letters and post cards. While I am not blaming that feature of the proposal of the Minister of Finance I very much doulbt whether he will receive from this source of taxation anything like the revenue which he ordinarily would receive or which he hopes to receive. We have had experience in regard to this matter in the past. We know what happened in 1896 and we know what happened in 1897 when the postal rate was reduced. We know that the postal revenue immediately jumped, that it kept [DOT]on 'bounding, and to-day it is away beyond what my hon. friend could have imagined it *would have been fifteen or sixteen years ago. I am afraid that the imposition of this additional fifty per cent in the case of letters and 100 per cent in the ease of post cards is going to defeat the object which the minister has in view. But if he feels that this is a proper method to adopt I dare say the rich man will pay his proportionate share of it. But there is a class of manufacturers and wealthy men which my hon. friend has not reached at all. Why has not my hon. friend levied a tax on the railways? There is not a railway in Canada that practically has not been built for the stockholders by the people of Canada.

Take the Grand
Trunk Pacific.

Certainlyl take the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if there is a railway in Canada that ought to pay a tax it is the Grand Trunk Pacific. The trouble is that when my hon. friends have something put up to them which they cannot answer they commence to jibe at it.
They cannot pay.

The Grand Trunk Pacific can pay, the Grand Trunk can pay, the Canadian Pacific Railway can pay and the Canadian Northern can pay. Every one of these railway systems has received practically every dollar put into it from the people of Canada, and they should be compelled to pay. But it would not suit my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to impose a tax upon those railway magnates. Why should not the street railway companies make some sacrifice to meet this horrible burden which my hon. friend is carrying upon his shoulders? Why should not the telegraph companies contribute something towards meeting the deficiency? 
Why should not the telephone companies pay something? There are few more flourishing corporations in Canada than the telephone companies, and they will flourish to a greater extent in the future, because there is no public utility which is being increased to a greater extent than is the telephone. Why has not my hon. friend imposed a tax upon express* companies? According to the investigation made by the Railway Commission a few years ago, it was demonstrated that the capital invested in an express company was practically nil, and that its profits were enormous. Why does not my hon. friend tax life insurance companies? For the life of me, I could not understand why he imposed a tax upon fire insurance companies and not upon life insurance companies. Why does he not impose a tax upon the large industrial corporations of Canada? He is giving his friends the manufacturers the right to charge the people of this country prices such as they never dreamt of before, and they are charging them and they will make enormous profits. Why does he not make them pay back some of the extra gains they will make as a result of this tariff? I suppose the answer is that it would not please his friends the manufacturers if he compelled them to pay something back into the treasury of the country.

How are the people
going to pay this 7J per cent tax to the treasury and also to the manufacturers?

That is exactly what 1 would like to know. How are they going to pay this 7i per cent tax when the other fellow pays nothing? My hon. friend does not appreciate my argument. I am finding fault with the Minister of Finance because he is making the people pay 7J per cent tax and letting the manufacturers go free. He should levy a direct tax on the magnates in such a, way that they cannot get hack at the people. Except in the case of the banks-and I am afraid that we shall pay the piper there-my hon. friend has imposed the tax in such a way that the magnates will get back at the people. Let the magnates stand some of the sacrifice which the ordinary people of this country are so willingly standing in order to work out this great war scheme.

That was not the question I asked. If the people pay the tax to the manufacturers, how are they going to pay it to any one else? You say that the

magnates get the benefit of the tax. If so, then the war tax is not paid by the people to any one else. That is clear.

is of no use to him. I fear that by these proposals the Minister of Finance is making the wall so high-and I think he had a shrewd suspicion of it himself-as to prevent the inflow of British goods into Canada, and so he will not only make the consumer in Canada pay more, but will injure the British manufacturer as well. And if there is a man to whom all Canadians, and all true British subjects, should look and whose interests should be guarded, it is the British manufacturer, the man who, as I have said, is the backbone of this war, the man who must pay the money, the man from whom the minister himself is borrowing every dollar that he is using in carrying on the war. There is no doubt that if you argue it as a matter of percentage only, there is a greater spread between the cost of seifding in American goods and the cost of sending in British goods than there was. But if you have made the wall so high that you are going to stop the import of both, then, though I would not find so much fault about stopping the American imports, we on this side do find fault-and that is the real object of the amendment-with anything that is done to hinder the British manufacturer from carrying on business and earning the money which he is so cheerfully paying for the purpose of this war.
I cannot make this thing plainer than by quoting a paragraph from the Ottawa Citizen. It refers first to a statement from the Toronto News, which newspaper, I think, was the originftor of this fallacious argument that the British preference is increased by these proposed duties, and then comments upon that .statement:
" The Daily News doss not argue, as the Ottawa Citizen contends, that the new tariff reduces the taxes on goods from Great Britain. It has said that the British preference is increased. As a matter of fact the taxation on foreign goods is increased by 7J per cent and on British goods by 5 per cent. This means 2j per cent increase in the preference."- Toronto News.
What the News then should say is that, relatively, the British preference is increased but, actually, it costs 5 per cent more to bring British goods into Canada than it did before Mr. White's war budget. Isn't that the case? And are we dealing in such matters with theories or with facts?
I need not elaborate further; the whole case is boiled down in that little paragraph. Is it not a fact that we are making somebody pay five cents on the dollar more to get British goods into Canada than before this tariff came into effect? I do not argue whether that is to be paid by the British manufacturer or by the Canadian consumer -somebody must pay it. And not only that
[Mr. Carvell.J
but somebody must pay on every article of a similar character that is manufactured in Canada.
There is another point which has already been dealt with and to Which I shall only refer, and that is the extra handicap upon British trade through increased freight and insurance. Surely these discouragements to trade between Britain and Canada should be enough without the Government taking the unpatriotic stand of raising higher the tariff wall against that trade. An hon. friend behind me reminds me of the freights on lumber. Of course, lumber does not come from Britain to Canada, but the increase in freights in lumber is an illustration of freights generally. When this war opened the freight on lumber was 2s. 6d. per standard. To-day it is 7s. 6d., or three times as great as it was eight months ago. And what is true of lumber going to Great Britain is true of cottons, woollens and other goods coming from Great Britain to Canada. It does seem that this should have been a sufficient burden upon British trade with Canada without this Government putting on an . additional 5 per cent which somebody must pay and which will discourage trade to that extent.
There was another matter to which I wished to refer, but I have already spoken longer than I had intended, and it is almost six o'clock. Let me summarize in a few words what I have already said. I tried to point out to the Minister of Finance the questions at issue between us. In the first place, if the Minister of Finance had carried on the affairs of the country with due regard to economy he would not have been compelled to raise additional revenues, because with the revenue which he would have raised in tlhe natural order of things he would have had a surplus and not a deficit. I pointed out that if there be an unfortunate condition of financial affairs the fault is not ours, but the burden of responsibility rests upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance. I have pointed out as best I could, that the result of his tariff proposals is not to encourage but to discourage trade, and not to increase revenue! but rather to decrease revenue; yet, though he is decreasing revenue he is increasing the cost of nearly every article that the ordinary man must use. I pointed out that another result will be to place an additional obstacle in the way of British trade with Canada. And if the Prime Minister thinks it necessary to read a lecture

to us, to throw out a challenge to the effect that if we persist in putting forward our views on these great financial problems in opposition to his, he will fight us and fight us at once-why, that is his business; it is a matter of entire indifference to us. We realize that the right hon. gentleman has the power to go to the country and have an election if he wishes to do so;-that is, if His Royal Highness has not the same mind on this subject as he is reported to have had in the month of August last. Let that be as it may, there is no use in a Prime Minister wielding the big stick and saying to us:	If you persist in putting forward
your views to the people and do it to the extent of compelling our people to vote, you will get a thrashing. We are prepared to take the thrashing or whatever else may come. If, on the other hand, the right hon. gentleman would take some of the ideas I have advanced-he says that nobody had given him an idea-let him remove the shackles from the producers of this country and put every man in a position to produce what he can. Let him remove from the ordinary consumers, the men who pay nine-tenths of the taxes, some of the burdens which now rest upon them, and put these new taxes, which we realize to be a sacrifice, upon the railways, the street railways, the telephones and telegraph companies, the express companies, the electric light and power companies, the great manufacturing concerns thus getting his revenue contributed by the men who have the money and the bank accounts and who are in a position to pay. Let him not wring it out of the poor people, many of whom are out of employment; many of whom are finding it an almost impossible task to make both ends meet. If the hon. gentleman will take some of these ideas to heart and bring them into play by resolving them into legislation, he will make a greater name for himself than he will ever make by playing the game with the manufacturers of this country. He will put the people of Canada in a position to contribute to the funds of the Red Cross Society and to other patriotic funds instead of paying this increased taxation. He will enable them to make easier and more pleasant the life of the men who are fighting in the trenches and he will put Canada in a position to do her share to bring to a successful termination the greatest war which this Empire or the world has ever seen.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, at every session of Parliament there is presented more or less legislation of the highest importance, but the most important of all is the Budget, for it establishes the policy under which the people of the country will have to live during the coming year and perhaps during many succeeding years. It is therefore no wonder that so many members on both sides of the House wish to place themselves on record as being in favour of or against the policy of the Government.
From wtoat I have gathered from the speeches already made on this important subject, I have concluded that two factors seem to have priority in the discussion, first, to all attacks made by the Opposition tne answer has been,- you have done worse or as badly. This to me, Sir, is small politics. Secondly, we have had lectures on social economy, plenty of theory, but so far very little practice, and the conclusion arrived at by hon. gentlemen opposite has been that the consumers of the country are satisfied, but this remains to be seen.
The hon. Minister of Finance in his Budget speech has exposed his new policy of taxation. I must say he did so in a dignified manner, in the only way that could be expected from a Minister of Finance, for the two most serious members of this House must always be the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. I am sorry to say, however, that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, instead of rising in the estimation of many, has perhaps descended some degrees after his last speech the other day. xi a speech of this nature had been delivered by the hon. Minister of Public Works for example, I for one would have thought him in his sphere; but for reasons that the hon. Minister of Puolic Works knows best it has not fallen Gris lot to do it. We are, Sir, in a' free country, and it is far from me to criticise the minister for the speech he has made.
Now, Sir, a new policy must be very effective in order to win the approval of the people of Canada, and to go to the root of the evil which forces the present policy on the country one would have to treat this question from three different points, that is from the domestic, social, and economic aspects, thus embracing all the arguments and reasons for or against this policy. It is not my intention to endeavour to give a

lecture^ on political economy for my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) has been kind enough to favour us with an elaborate one. During his remarks I was very interested in his theory and and I must say that for many of the theories he enunciated in the House I have great respect. In many instances I was absolutely in accord with him. But we must bear in mind that it is with practice that we must deal at the present time, we must take the conditions as they are, we must deal with the mentality of people developed under the present conditions; we must bear in mind that the citizens composing our population must be looked after, all our institutions must be educated into a more democratic spirit, and a certain amount of the productive power of the people must be returned to them until such time as they can get all they are entitled to. I say to the hon. member for Peterborough that there are others beside himself who believe in that policy. But, Sir, I say that we have an immediate duty to fulfil, that is to prevent oppression. Every one in the House or out of it, would favour any measure which would have for its object the relief from oppression of the masses and the consumers of the country. That is the great question at issue and I am sorry to say that, as far as I am concerned, the effect of this new policy will be to pauperize the masses. Much has been said about taxes. It is not my intention to go over the ground that has already been covered. My hon. friend from Car-leton (Mr. Carvell) this afternoon spoke of taxes and so did the right hon. Prime Minister; but when he spoke d the tax on railway tickets it came to my mind that poor people are bound to be more affected by the tax on railway tickets than anybody else. Of course I will admit that if there was 100 per cent difference in the cost of a first-class and second-class ticket, if a first-class ticket were worth exactly double the price of a second-class ticket, then the poor man would not be so badly affected. If one pays $2 for a ticket and another pays $4.95, there is no difference whatever in the amount of taxes that will be imposed on the two tickets. Of course, it may be said that is a very small item, but still the Minister of Finance expects to derive a certain amount of revenue from it. If I understand correctly, the railway companies are to be permitted to collect this particular tax, and I assume that, for their trouble in collecting the tax, they will not have to pay anything to the 
Government. If that be true, the railway companies have no reason to complain. Of course a pullman is a luxury that the poor man rarely enjoys, so that will not affect him much. I shall not deal with this tax at any greater length, because it has already been discussed by many members in this House. The Finance Minister also expects to raise quite a bit on stamps. I take issue with him on that point. I know that a certain large corporation in my own city of Montreal which sends out a lot of mail has engaged young boys to distribute their mail from door to door, and I suppose the same thing will be done by other large corporations. In fact, they will really save by the imposition of this stamp tax. If the practice I have spoken of is followed in the large cities of Canada, the Finance Minister will get very much less than he expects from this particular tax.
I should also like to say a few words about the tax on patent medicines, a tax which will surely affect the poor people more than anybody else. When a rich man has anybody sick in his house he generally calls in a doctor; but the poor man cannot afford that, and if any one in his house falls sick the first thing he resorts to is patent medicine. It is the poor people, and they are the largest class in this country, whom this tax will most affect. It may be said that the druggists will not charge any more for these patent medicines, but commercial men are all alike; they are in business to make money, and I do not blame them for it. The legislation of this country permits them to do it. Directly this tax comes into force, or very soon after, the customer will be charged that much extra for his patent medicine, and as the customers are mostly from the poor classes this tax will bear most heavily on them.
A tax has also been imposed on spirits. Speaking for myself, I would favour the passing of legislation by this House to prevent the manufacture of at altogether. That is how I feel about it. As foT the tax on banks, the Minister of Finance has stated -I speak under correction-that the Bank of Montreal, which will be the largest contributor, will pay $150,000 a year. But that is but a drop in the bucket to the Bank of Montreal, and other large financial institutions. It seems to me that, if a revenue tax has to be imposed, these large institutions should be made to contribute more than that. I do not complain very much of these particular taxes, because it is my intention to submit to the

minister before I get through, that a revenue tax or a direct tax, if necessary, should be imposed, and the tariff left entirely alone.
We must remember that during a depression, the policy should be, not to increase, but to diminish all budgets, whether domestic, (social or political. In this House and out of it, on the public platform, and through all the newspapers, we have been preaching economy. Many citizens who were paying taxes in some form or other have had to save to the very limit, but it seems that the Government does not realize the present (Situation. To administer the public affairs by increasing the tariff, is not keeping pace with present economic conditions.
All hon. members who have spoken on -the other side of the House have condemned the -attitude of members on this side, and have said that large public works in time of stress are demanded by the working men of the country. That is so, but the amount of money asked for on account of public works will not all be spent this year. The workingmen of this country know that it is -a physical impossibility to (spend that -amount. I want to tell my hon. friend, and the Government generally, that the amount asked for for public works cannot be spent during this coming year. According to the information I have gathered, and -after looking up the re-votes, I feel sure that we could save at least $6,000,000 in the Public Works Department. Up to the time I came into this House I had spent all my life in the building tr-adie, -and I can -speak with knowledge of building. Suppose -a $50,000 building is to be erected somewhere. First of all the plans have to be prepared. There is a lot of red tape about that, and it generally takes about two months. Then tenders have to be called for and announcements made in newspapers in different parts of Canada. Plans have to be deposited in some city where the contractors may submit their tenders. After a certain time the tenders are sent to Ottawa, and after quite a long time they are opened. Then there is another lapse of time before the contracts are awarded. I believe I am well within the limit when I say that it takes four or five and probably six months before work can be started on that building. Therefore, on a $50,000 building-and I am taking a pretty large one-the amount spent in one year could not be more than $10,000; and if that is so, why should we vote $50,000 when only $10,000
is needed for the year? The same thing applies to all the public buildings, and I am sure that if we voted just what would be spent in one year we could save quite a few million dollars on public works. In some cases, no doubt, all the money voted will be spent during the year, but where it will not be spent the labour men of this country will derive little benefit from the money - voted. In most cases it will be a physical impossibility to spend the whole amount voted.
I thought that I would put this question clearly before the House. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) knows probably better than I do that it is impossible for him to spend all the money on public buildings and other works in connection with the present Budget.
I want to speak of the policy of made-in-C'anada. Having reference to the present conditions and to the proposed increase in the tariff I say that this is the biggest farce that the human brain ever invented. It is the best possible weapon that could be handed to the manufacturer to enable him' to deceive the people. It is the best system by which an unscrupulous wholesaler or retailer can dishonestly put certain goods on the market. It is the best device possible to enable unscrupulous employers to oppress their employees. I will give an example. I hope that I shall not be asked to mention the store to which I refer as I do not want to hurt any one. There is a certain store in a large city in which a considerable number of young men and girls have been employed to remove the words, " made in Germany " from a lot of goods and to mark them, "made in Canada". I have proof and I know whereof I speak. You are putting it in the power of any manufacturer, storekeeper, wholesaler or retailer, at any time to do likewise. That is why I say it furnishes these people with an opportunity to put certain goods on the market that are not what they purport to be. It is a farce and it is not in keeping with our present commercial system.
It enables the manufacturer to charge whatever price he sees fit. It will hamper and destroy our present system of transportation and reduce to a minimum the earning power of the workers in the different branches of industry. The unscrupulous employer and dealer will, if he sees fit, buy elsewhere and sell his goods as being goods made in Canada. It will afford an opportunity to place upon the market inferior

goods and sell them at exorbitant prices notwithstanding the fact that our manufacturers enjoy a high measure of protection. I will admit that it may open a few industries but it will help to merge our industries into new combinations and put prices out of reach. The Government cannot be in favour of such a policy because if they were we would have to go back to the policy of 1911, and it would mean that they would have to favour free markets and reciprocity.
I would like for a moment to touch on the tax on coal. I do not refer to anthracite coal because anthracite coal comes in free. Anthracite coal has become to a large extent a luxury in the large cities. The prices asked for anthracite coal at certain times of the year are such that the poor man cannot buy it. If he has to buy by the hundred pounds, as many have to do in the cities, he pays as high as $15 or $16, or probably more, a ton. You may say that the question of the duty on bituminous coal will not affect the people in the cities. I have heard it stated that bituminous coal is not burned in the large cities. Since anthracite coal has become a luxury, coke is being more largely used by the consumers. They are buying coke instead of anthracite coal.
I do not believe that the companies selling that coke to the consumer will not add to the price of the coke the increase in the tariff rate on bituminous coal. It has been stated that the consumer will be affected by the tariff on bituminous coal by reason of the gas that he will burn, but there are a great number of families in the citis who do not know anything about gas. Therefore, my conclusion is that the increase in the tariff rates will affect them by reason of the coke which they burn.
I want to say a few words on the tax on raw materials. I will give an example to illustrate my view. I claim raw materials which we cannot get in this country should not be taxed. The other day my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), during the course of his speech, read a letter. I do not know whether he read all of the letter to the House; but, whether what I refer to was in the letter or not, I know exactly what has happened. My hon. friend read a letter written by some of the potters at St. John and he said that they were satisfied with the 5 per cent increase in the preferential tariff. It is true that they have a protection of 5 per cent against goods coming from Great Britain and with this the men were satisfied-, When the 5 per cent

in the preferential rate was announced in the House by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, these very men of whom my hon. friend from Peterborough spoke, went to their employers at St. John and said: You have lowered our wages and you have told us that if you had only 6 per cent protection you could give us the same wages that you gave us formerly. What was the answer? The answer was: We are very sorry, but we cannot give you an increase because they are charging us 5 per cent on the raw material. I am giving an instance that was brought before this House, but it was not quite complete. There was only one side of it presented to the House. If that is what has happened in this particular case I do not see why it will not happen in other cases. If the manufacturers of this country could be trusted-I do not think they can be because I have not found any yet that I could trust in this matter-to charge only 5 per cent ad valorem increase on the raw material that went into the finished goods it would be a very small fraction that would be added to the cost of the goods. The claim has been made that it was impossible for the Canadian manufacturer of cotton to manufacture it as cheaply as it can be manufactured ^in the United States. If a bale of cotton is transported from the southern states to the New England states, and if another bale is transported from the southern states to the city of Montreal, I am sure, although I have not the figures, that there will be no- difference whatever in the cost of transportation as between the two bales. That raw material used to come in free. The machinery that is used in the manufacture of cotton in Montreal and in the United States is exactly alike. Power is as cheap in Canada as in the United States and labour is cheaper. How is it then that the manufacturers of cotton claim that it is not possible to manufacture cotton as cheaply in Canada as they do on the other side of the line? A royal commission some few years ago made an investigation, and they sat at Valleyfield.
I have not beside me a copy of the report of the commission but I read it at the time and these manufacturers were so ashamed of their profits that they had to charge a large amount of money to repairs to buildings which never was expended on any work of that kind.
The manufacturers are going to take advantage of the 5 per cent on the raw material and also of the 7) per cent on the finished article. During the last year or two the price of labour has diminished.

Labour is not, paying as well as it was a couple of years ago, and, of course, not as well as last year. Therefore the manufacturers are going to be protected, first, by the 5 per cent duty on raw material; secondly, by the 7J per cent duty on the finished article, and then by how much per cent on the diminished wages? I claim that they are going to be protected by 20 to 22J per cent. That is too high a protection. The burden of the protectionist system is supposed to be borne by outsiders; hut that is a fallacy, because protectionists are getting rich while the poorer classes are getting poorer. The Government derives only a small benefit, and the public pays ten times as much as the Government receives. A great professor of political economy has exposed that fallacy very clearly.
My hon. friend the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) has discussed the question of the preferential tariff, and it is not my intention to go over that ground again.
Several hon. members spoke of the home market. We are subsidizing the railway companies and also the ocean transportation lines. We are doing it for a certain purpose, namely, for the purpose of transportation. We are not doing it for the purpose of transportation from Nova Scotia to Montreal; we are doing it for the purpose of transportation across the ocean. If we are going to take such an active interest in the home market, we should stop subsidizing those ocean transportation lines. Not only for the present, but for some years to come, there is going to be great difficulty In transportation across the Atlantic, because so many vessels are tied up. Therefore I would not be surprised if, at the next session of Parliament, we were to offer further subsidies to transportation companies. If we should have to do that, then the policy of an increase in the preferential tariff is absolutely wrong.
It has been said that the manufacturers will not increase prices. I believe that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) stated that an industrial establishment of which he knew, although he.did not mention the name, had recalled its prices and that in future it was going to have lower prices. It just happens that I know something about that industry, because 1 put in twenty-eight years at it. That is nothing new for that industry. There is a combine of the manufacturers of hot water boilers and radiators. The prices are set every year, and no manufacturer is able to sell below those
prices to the wholesalers or to the retailers. It has been the custom for the combine, when trade is bad, to change the prices. The manufacturers can well afford to do so. It may be said that this company or another company is willing to give an extra 5 per cent. The manufacturers will say: Our price is $100; the discount is 40 per cent, with an extra 10 per cent and an extra 5 per cent and so on. The public at large will say: 40 and 10 and 5 make 55, and they believe that the discount is 55 per cent. I do not want to give the figures, but I wiU let my hon. friend work them out. The extra 5 per cent discount is not a very great amount on the price of a commodity.
I have under my hand something showing the effect of the proposed change in the tariff. I have here a letter from Ames-Holden, McOready, Limited, under date of March 1, 1915, giving prices on shoes. I will put it on Hansard:
We beg to advise that the recent increase oi 75 per cent in the Canadian customs tariff on imported raw and other materials which enter into' the cost of manufacturing shoes, compels us to advance our selling prices. This is without taking into consideration the higher and increasing cost of leather due to the enormous demand for war purposes.
We have, however, decided that on account of having a stock of materials on hand, not to change our quotations until we are obliged to do so, at which time a new price list will be issued. Orders now in our hands to be shipped, will be filled at prices at which the goods were sold.
We consider it due to our customers to advise them of the above, instead of advancing prices without notice, and will be pleased to execute all orders for your immediate'requirements at present prices, and any business you can favour us with will receive our very best attention and service. Our service means prompt deliveries and fair treatment. Thanking you for past favours,
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd) Ames Holden McCready, Limited.
My hon. friend the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) discussed the question of shoes this afternoon and it is not my intention to go over the same ground again.
It would probably be interesting to learn the opinions of some men outside of the Old Country in regard to the effect of a high tariff on the mass of the consumers. I will read a few lines of the evidence given by American ship-owners before the United States Commission on the Mercantile Marine. This is the effect on trade as given by Mr. Austin Taylor, M.P.:
Protection has been destructive to shipping. The percentage of American trade carried in American bottoms fell from 72.5 in 1860 to 9-2 in 1900. The ocean-going tonnage of America

diminished from 2,600,000 tons in 1861 to less than 900,000 in 1903.
So far as transportation is concerned, it -[DOT] is plain that if there is a diminution, less labour must be employed.
Let us see what Mr. Ashley says in his " Tariff History." He gives remarkable figures proving beyond a doubt that the present policy is not one to better existing conditions. He points out that in the United States protection has been from the beginning a settled policy. It has been associated with sound principle on many subjects. It has stood for the honest payment of national debts, for free labour as against slave labour, for high wages for the American labourer. But in that country protection has not given to the workers all the advantages which might have been expected. More than twenty-nine millions of persons are occupied for gain and less than one million benefit by protection.
Australia is often set forth as an example and, in case some hon. members have forgotten the effect of tariffs in that country, let me give an example of free trade and protection. Lord Goschen gives us some startling figures on this subject. Until the Commonwealth was established Australia offered to students of economics an ooject lesson of singular interest. \ ictoria and New South Wales were neighbouring states, not urssimilar in climate and resources. Both countries made their beginning under a free trade system, Victoria being far ahead of New South Wales in manufacturing industries. In 1866 Victoria became protectionist; New South v>
ales adhered to free trade. Now, compare the conditions m 1902. Number of employed in Victoria, males 47,059, females 19,470- total 66,529; New South Wales, males 54,451, females, 11,674-total 66,135. New South Wales, the free trade state, employed more than eight thousand fewer women than did Victoria. Now, look at the value of output. In Victoria it was $98,000,000, and in New South Wales $121,500,000. These figures do not prove that 'protection is a blessing.
The policy proposed by the Finance Minister to-day means increase of taxes on nearly all articles, including food. Now, whether a man is rich or poor, he must feed his family, or at least he must make the attempt. During the last two years many have not been able to find work at which they could earn wages with which to buy food, and conditions of late have been such that you could not buy a job for any money. Many to-day are going to the front

to procure food for their families through separation allowance and the patriotic fund, and on those who are left behind we impose the extra burden. Sir John Gorst tells us that if we tax food a number of those who are now above the poverty line will sink below it, and those already below it will sink yet lower. And he goes on to say- and here I would ask our imperialist friends to think it over-that free importation of food is vital to the physical and moral wellkeeping of the nation, and is therefore at the root of true imperialism. A great imperial power cannot be founded on a starved and degraded population. These ideas should appeal to the Minister of Finance, but whether they do or not, I am sure they will appeal strongly to the wage earners of the country.
Now, I ask myself whether hon. gentlemen opposite are well satisfied with the present condition. I do not think they are. I do not think in their heart and soul they are satisfied. They may say: Our present policy will better conditions. That remains to be seen. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition foresaw the condition of this country and endeavoured to meet that condition by his policy of 1911. If every other member of this House were against that famous policy, there would be one at least in favour of it-myself. I have never seen yet an economic reason that could be given against that famous policy; and I have no hesitation in saying that, while probably depression would have come upon us in any case, it would not have been so severe a9 it is at present had that policy been adopted. We are told present conditions are caused by the war. The more I study the present economic condition, the less I can see that the war is responsible for it. There are many reasons, as many of my hon. friends know; and one reason, as I have stated, I strongly believe was the nonacceptance of the policy of 1911. Any one, whether in this House or out of it, who lured the people wrongly away from that policy is well punished to-day.
The unemployed problem is the object of the thoughts of every one in every walk of life. We were promised a commission on the high cost of living. When that commission was appointed by the Government, I stated that I was in favour of it, but that I did not expect that it would ever report. Had we had the report of that commission, it might have helped us to a better understanding of present conditions. But if that

commission operated in other cities as it operated in my own, I confess that I have no great hopes from its report. The members of that commission came to the city of Montreal, and, I may almost say, locked themselves up in a room in the Windsor hotel and had a few men come and give evidence before them. But not a single labour man of any kind was asked to go before that commission. These who were most directly affected, those who could give the most valuable information to the commission, were ignored altogether. It was a commission in favour of the manufacturer, and not in favour of the labourer.
Another thing of which my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition saw the necessity some years ago-and I do not think that under the circumstances my hon. friends can say anything to the contrary-was the establishment of shipbuilding industries in the western, central and eastern portions of Canada. If these industries were now established, what would it mean for the unemployed ? When the war is over there will be a gTeat demand for shipbuilding; the only place in which shipbuilding is carried on to any extent at the present time is Montreal. Other ships than warships are needed. When the great demand for ships for commercial purposes .arises, I fear that Canada will be far behind all the other nations in the matter of shipbuilding, and if shipbuilding industries are not established in Canada we shall have to go to the United States for our ships.'
I can tell the House exactly how the workingmen feel in regard to this matter. The workingmen all over Canada voice their opinion in regard to my hon. friend's proposals in this manner:	so far as the
war is concerned, we have done more than our share; we have furnished our flesh and blood to the extent of at least 80 per cent of all contingents which have gone or will go. We have made more sacrifices than other classes of the community; it cannot be said that we are disloyal. Many of us who go to the front will leave behind widows and orphans. We do not mind the suffering; those who .come .after us will know that we fought and died for their liberties and for the true principle of democracy. We know that those who are in the trenches desire that these taxes be imposed not upon -those whom they have left behind, but upon the great financial institutions and corporations, which are able to pay.
The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) stated the other day that the workingmen were satisfied with these proposals. I do not believe that the hon. gentleman had a mandate from them to say that they were satisfied. Surely he could not	say	they are	satisfiedin the city of Toronto and in the other	large	cities of	Canada.
Far from it. It is absolutely unfair to say that the workingmen and the farmers are satisfied. I do not know enough about farming conditions to say whether or not the farmers are satisfied, but I am sure that if the hon. member for South Toronto had given due thought to the matter, he would not have said that the workingmen of Canada approve the proposals.
We all understand that the present deficit has to be met in some way. I am afraid I cannot say that the deficit is d^e to the economy that has been practised by the Government. To meet this deficit, according to the Minister of Finance, a direct and indirect tax is to be imposed. This is where I take issue with my hon. friend and with the Government, because,
9 p.m as I have said, the imposition of these taxes will bear too heavily upon the masses of the consumers. When one criticises a mode of taxation, he should, in all fairness, suggest a remedy. The remedy that I suggest is the imposition of income taxes, and, if need be, direct taxes. There is no reason why the man who earns say $1,000 should not make a definite contribution out of that amount towards defraying the expenses of war. If that were done, each man would know how much he contributes; under the proposed system no one will know how much money he pays into the treasury. A poor man who has a family of five or six children will pay a larger amount in taxes than the rich man who has a small family, or none at all. The great proportion of these new taxes will be paid by the farmers and the workingmen of the country. I do not say that the rich man will not pay a share, but it is well known that a great proportion of the population of Canada consists of farmers and workingmen, so that they will have to bear the greatest share of the burden.
Mr. R. Hunter, a well-known sociologist, in a volume recently published, has the following to say with respect to the effect of high tariffs in the United States:
In Boston, in 1903, twenty per cent of the people were in distress. Fourteen per cent of the families in the city of Manhattan were evicted in the same year. Ten per cent of those who died in Manhattan had pauper burials. There seems to be reason to believe that the number of those in poverty in New

York and in other large cities and industrial centres rarely falls below '15 per cent of the population.
It is not our intention, I hope, to take any steps which will cause the conditions which prevail in those large American cities-conditions which have been caused by the imposition of high tariffs. Conditions of a similar character have existed in other countries. In Great Britain some few years ago, when it became necessary to raise additional revenue, a great man spoke from the ranks of Government saying': We are going to tax those who can best afford to pay. The land tax scheme, which was then proposed, was severely criticised by the moneyed men of Britain. The Government went to the people on that issue; all the moneyed interests of Britain opposed the scheme, #>ut the majority of the people approved it and the Government was returned. Let me come down to more recent years, the time of the last presidential election in the United States. Mr. Wilson was a Unversity man, a student of political economy; and he knew that the high tariff in the United States was the cause of the existing depression. What did he do? He reduced the tariff of his country and imposed an income tax. Again, Sir, the big financial elements were against him, but they are now commencing to understand that his policy was the only sound policy to adopt. It may be said in the House that he has not reduced his tariff very much; but if I remember rightly the reduction in tariff that he made amounted to $80,000,000 and the income tax that he imposed on the people of the United States amounted to $83,000,000. So then there was just as much money to administer public affairs, and to-day the people are fairly well satisfied. I was in the United States last year and heard very few complaints. This is what we call democracy, and if President Wilson's action has been for the benefit of democracy, I claim that what Lloyd George did in England was for tlhe benefit of democracy.
We might come right down to the inception of the war to show what great men will sometimes do for democracy. When war was declared between the Allies and Germany there was one member of the ruling order in Europe, one of the crowned heads of Europe, of whom we had (heard very little. It just happens that I have read the history of that great man, and it is no wonder that when the war broke out the spirit of democracy of King A'bert of Bel-

gium showed itself and that Ihe rose fully to the great needs of the occasion, as has been said in this House before, and has saved the situation for the Allies. Democracy is bound to get the best of autocracy, and what is the underlying principle of the present war? It is democracy against the Prussian autocracy. I might go farther and demonstrate that great men are bound to spring up at critical moments to the height of any situation. When the Allies had to find one or two men to guide the destinies of those great armies, we all knew of General French, a great man, able to face the situation; but very few of us had ever heard the name Joffre. But that great general has shown himself to be equal to the situation, and I take the word of General French that Joffre is not only a great warrior but a great man.

It does not appear to
me, after listening to the hon. gentleman for some time, that he is keeping very close to the motion before the House.

Do I understand that
when I speak of the tariff, etc., I am within the limit?
