Yes.
Mr. VERVILnE:	Do I understand also
that if I can say that great men will arise to the height of the situation as far as Canada is concerned I am also in order? That is what I want to get at! I do not want to go beyond that. I wish to show that great men are likely to arise at certain moments to safeguard the interests of the country, as far as tariffs are concerned-and I have almost finished. The Minister of Finance has thought himself big enough to meet the situation today and he has exposed to us a certain policy, I must congratulate my hon. friend on believing that he was equal to the situation; but at the same time I for one am not prepared to say that tne policy which my hon. friend has presented will meet the present situation. I am happy to say that at least one hon. member in this House has risen to tne situation and has seen and felt this current of democracy that covers the country. I have been in this House for nine years. I have listened to a great many speeches, and very good and sensible ones, from both sides of the House; but never in my short period of parliamentary life have I listened to a speech more democratic in spirit and feeling, more in accordance with present conditions than that of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid

Laurier). He has risen to the height of the situation, hut like the great Englishman I have mentioned, he has announced his intention, as far as it is in the power of the leader of the Opposition to do so; and 1 am confident that the labour men of the country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, when they read his speech and study its meaning will not hesitate to ask him to put in operation what he has so well announced and from tnat day we may expect to have enacted legislation for the benefit of the masses.

Mr
Speaker, it is obvious that at this late hour one cannot hope to add very much to the subject matter of the debate that has engaged the attention of the House during the last few days, in fact, during the past few weeks. I venture to state that a stranger coming to this House and looking down from the gallery would have a very great deal of difficulty to discover just what this House was discussing. The stranger listening to hon. gentlemen on the other side would be impressed with the fact that we were very much concerned about a domestic issue, questions of extravagance, questions of tariff. It is the same old story, the same old cant, the same old hypocrisy, the same old cry of extravagance, the same old appeal to the passions and the prejudices of the people, the same old attempt to arouse class against class, the same old effort to arouse the agrarian population against the manufacturers of Canada, the same old appeal to arouse the West against the East that I have listened to for the last fifteen years; the same old tale of the privileged classes and of the alleged wealthy classes; the same old solicitude or affected solicitude for the masses; the same long dismal wail and tale that was listened to in this country up until 18%; and that we have listened to since 1911; and the same old appeal in another Chamber of this Parliament to the racial and language passions and prejudicies of a portion of the people of this country. I must confess that, when this great conflict broke out, I expected and hoped that much would happen to bring unity between the East and West, between the eastern manufacturer and the western farmer; and there were signs, strong signs too, that such a result was about to be attained. For the grain growers and the manufacturers met together and discussed their common questions, and in the light of this great conflict forgot many of their differences. It remained for hon. gentlemen opposite once 69
more to precipitate into the politics of this country, at this time, after we had had a very considerable truce and the promise of a long-continued one, the controversy, conflict, passions and prejudices that have long been incident to their discussion of public questions and of fiscal measures.
How can one characterize the long and dismal wail that we have listened to for the last few weeks? There has been nothing constructive, nothing offered by which to accelerate the raising of the revenue, or by which to deal with the great problems that confront this country at this time. It has been one long criticism, one long tirade of abuse against the powers that be, one long attempt at destruction. There has been no offer of a constructive measure, and no offer or attempt to support the Administration in this great crisis of this country's affairs. I venture to think, Mr. Speaker, that the language of Lord Tennyson more accurately describes the situation than any words of mine could:
An infant crying in the night,
An infant crying for the light,
Ani with no language hut a cry.
It is true that trade has been dislocated, that the great centres of the world's commerce have been disturbed. It is true exchanges have been closed in the great markets and centres of the world. It is true, and I regret to say it is true, but it is one of the incidents of a great war, that great accumulations of funds by the banks have taken place; for if the panic-stricken depositor demands his money the bank must be in a position to hand back what belongs to him. That confronts every country in circumstances such as these. It is true that there has been restriction of credits, and a lessening of trade. All these things have taken place, but they are not blamable to this Government. We know that it has long been the habit and custom of men in normal times, to blame-or praise governments for good and bad times. Sometimes the Government in power has assumed all the vir-. tues that attach to good times and when there has been a long continued series of lean years the Opposition has often blamed the Government for it. I remember reading in the biography of an English statesman that when Disraeli had been defeated and succeeded by Mr. Gladstone, the rural labourers said:	"When old Beaconsfield
was gaffer there was none of them hard times." And when Gladstone came into power and there was a succession of lean



years the opposite was said by those who opposed that Government. That is bound to be so. That is so in the United States. It is so in Canada. Oppositions blame governments for lean years and bad times. But governments have nothing more to do with good times or bad times, considered from the standpoint of world movements, than had Pharaoh's chief butler or baker to do with the emaciated condition of the shadowy kine.	_ -
But there is good and just cause for the condition which prevails in Canada at this time. Canada, as part of the British Empire, is at war. It does seem to me, and has seemed so ever since this war began, that we Canadians are slow, to realize that we are at war. For a century we have lived at peace; for a century we have lived side by side at peace with the greatest neighbour that a country can live beside. There have been no forts and no fortresses, and that very fact has accustomed us to think of peace, and not to realize what war with all its sadness and sorrow means. But the slackening of tyade, the lessening of credits, the destruction of many things, have brought home to us the fact that we are at war; and there are other and more cogent reasons that are bringing to our mind every day the fact that Canada is at war. Who, reading the daily press and studying the casualty lists that are coming home to us in these dark and grim days, can fail to realize that this Canada of ours is as much at war as any part of the British Empire? There are no words that I can use that would so adequately express the meaning I have in mind as the beautiful imagery of John Bright when he said:
An Angel of Death has heen abroad throughout the land. You can almost hear the beating of his wings. There is no one, as when the first-born were slain of old, to sprinkle with blood the lintel and the two side posts of our doors that he may spare and pass on. He takes his victims from the castle of the noble, the mansion of the wealthy, and the cottage of the poor and lowly.
Aye, Mr. Speaker, that brings home to us ns nothing else could the fact that this country is at war. But the measure of our ability to participate in this great conflict must be the limit of our resources in men and treasure. The human element has been willing. Speaking as a western man, there is nothing that fills one with greater pride and pleasure than to see the splendid way in which the men have responded to the call of the Empire. In the province in

which I live I venture to think that not less than 12,000 men, out of a population of less than 450,000, have offered their services to the King and Empire. The human element has responded. It is for us in Parliament assembled to provide the necessary money with which that human element may be made effective on the field of battle. To participate in this great war involves the expenditure of vast sums of money, for war nowadays cannot be conducted without, money, and it is for the people's representatives in Parliament assembled to raise the money wherewith that conflict may be carried on, that the men who have so willingly offered their services may be able to give their best in the cause of this Empire and for the cause of humanity. It is of course an enormous burden to cast upon tihe Government. I venture to think that never in the history of eight millions of people occupying so vast an area have any men 'been charged with so large a responsibility as that which has devolved upon this Government. We are prone sometimes to be critical, sometimes to be censorious; but I have learned tlhe lesson that, while it is easy to criticise and easy to be censorious, it is not always easy to accomplish the vast undertakings that this country has begun and carried forward so successfully since this war began. In all the history of this world I venture to challenge any hon. gentleman opposite to point to a single instance where a Government, suddenly confronted with so vast a responsibility, with obligations so great, has been able to discharge those obligations so successfully as to win to some extent the gratitude and admiration of mankind. But, Sir, it is the duty of an Opposition to criticise. I listened to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition in August last, say to this House that while he claimed the right, and properly so, to criticise all that might be done by this Government, he proposed to give to them the best assistance he could, in order that they might carry forward to a successful conclusion the obligations and responsibilities which then rested upon them. I rejoiced to think that it was so, and I still think it is the duty of the Opposition fearlessly to criticise wherever occasion invites or demands. But, Sir, sometimes there are larger duties and obligations cast upon an Opposition. There comes a time when men must forget that they are party men, and must remember only that they are the chosen representatives of the people charged with the duty to assist in devising ways and

means by which this conflict may be carried to a successful conclusion.
We have been reminded of what has taken place in the Motherland. We have been reminded that leaders of the Opposition there have been consulted by Mr. Asquith in reference to the conduct of the war. I have failed in any study I have been able to give to the subject to find that Mr. Asquith at any time consulted the leaders of the Opposition in reference to or concerning any Budget proposals that were about to be submitted to the people of Great Britain. It has never been done in so far as I have been able to find, but it is true that Mr. Asquith had occasion to consult and consider with his opponents the different measures affecting the well-being, not only of the British Isles, but the adjustment of financial difficulties and trade arrangements of world wide importance. It is true he did, but surely this House has not forgotten that Mr. Asquith was in a position to discuss these questions with a Balfour, a Chamberlain, a Lansdowne or a Bonar Law. There is a difference. It is true that in the final analysis the Government must be held responsible for the proposals it submits to Parliament. I have not yet heard of any Government that cared to consider with the Opposition the character of the fiscal proposals which should be submitted to Parliament, and I venture to think that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, in his address, had not reference to the Budget or to fiscal matters, but rather to those matters of larger and more general application to which I have just referred.
Now, the Government has accepted the responsibility of submitting to Parliament fiscal measures. It is absolutely certain that if we are going to carry forward this work, if this country is going to take its part in maintaining free democracy, if we are going to carry fprward this struggle on behalf of humanity, if we propose to do these things, then we must have the sinews of war, and it is equally true and cannot be denied that fresh taxes must be resorted to in order that the money may be raised. A great English Chancellor of the Exchequer once, speaking under circumstances somewhat similar to those confronting this Government, said that the prime duty of the Government is to look for revenue, and the ideal tax is that which will yield most revenue with the least injury and inconvenience to the community and without any injurious or oppressive burden on any industry or any class. He further said that taxation should be so framed that when
peace returned it would provide also for ordinary expenditure, and have no injurious effects in placing the fiscal system on a basis which would be equitable to every class in the community.
That is the principle which -a great English Chancellor of the Exchequer thought worthy of consideration in dealing with problems such as those which now confront the Minister of Finance. In the United Kingdom the Chancellor of the Exchequer can usually provide for a tax upon some object or article of almost universal consumption which will ensure a very large and buoyant revenue. For instance, in the Crimean war Tesort was had to raising taxes by an increased duty on tea and on sugar, and iso during all these years duties have been imposed upon articles of universal consumption, and they have been sufficient to yield a large and buoyant revenue. But in Canada the population is too limited. We have not the same large population, and there is no article of almost universal consumption, that enables the Government with certainty to select that article, impose a tax upon it and raise the large revenue that will be necessary for the purpose of carrying on the war. It is true, however, that in this instance the Minister of Finance, wittingly or unwittingly,-and I choose to believe that he did it wittingly-had regard to the words of the leader of the Opposition last year in framing his fiscal measure, and also had regard to the party truce that was supposed to exist. What did he do ? Instead of looking about to see what one single article, or two articles, or three articles, he might increase the duty upon, he said: I will not do that because it will involve a discussion of the tariff as a whole; I will content myself with adding something to the rate on all articles or nearly all articles that are imported. In order to prevent criticism and in order to prevent it being said that he had embarked upon a new policy for war purposes, be imposed a uniform increase by this tariff of 5 and 7i per cent. Surely nothing better could be calculated to disarm criticism or promote unity and peace. The tariff we have before us to-day is the tariff of 1907. It is the tariff placed upon the statute books by the (right hon. gentleman and the party opposite. It is the tariff which was represented to us as being the acme of excellence, the tariff that had been made upon scientific principles, an almost perfect tariff. Then, if that be so, if we have already made and placed upon the statute

statescraft! Great intelligent patriotism! Pure loyalty and regard for the country! When they see a party advantage, because they hope these taxes will prove unpopular, they oppose them.
They say to us that we could curtail our expenditure. It is not a theory that confronts this country, it is a condition. Are partially-roofed buildings to be left uncovered?-partly completed public buildings to be left open for the elements to destroy?- bridges that partially span streams to be left unfinished? Is every part of the public service to be neglected, or is the Government to be carried on? Are post offices, armouries, and great public undertakings not to be provided for? Are railways and bridges not to be completed?-aye, and more, are the great terminal facilities now in process of construction not to be finished, primarily that the traffic that we now have and expect in western Canada may be taken care of? No other part of the Dominion is more deeply interested than western Canada in the completion of the great terminal facilities at Halifax and Vancouver; in the completion of the canals; in the spanning of the. St. Lawrence that the Transcontinental may be of some value to the state. If that highway stops at Quebec, obviously it can be used for but a few months in the year. If it is to become a great public highway, and if it is to meet the public needs, it must be carried across the St. Lawrence to reach the great seaports of St. John and Halifax. The Government realizes that you cannot stop these works. Half-completed undertakings must be carried through. Can they find a man in the West, or a man in all Canada who will say: if you exercise a little more economy, if you left works half finished, left them hung up in the air, you would not have to resort to increased taxation? Do they underestimate the intelligence of the country or not? I do not believe that there is a man in Canada who would be misled by such prattle as that; that there is a single elector who would be deluded by such nonsensical sophistry.
These are the questions we have to consider. They say to us: if you could not limit your expenditure on capital account, while you might have gone forward and completed these great undertakings, you are paying too many clerks; there is no necessity for war taxes; you have one man too many at ?75 a month; take him off and there is no need for war taxes. That is the little

five-eent picayune politics that we hear of from these hon. gentlemen.

There are ten thousand

Hon. gentlemen say that this proposal takes away the British preference. I shall not deal with that argument because it was dealt with very fully by my right hon. friends the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) and therefore any ' observations I might make would be mere surplusage. But not only has the British preference been increased by the placing of a duty upon raw material, not only has that
been done by the difference between 5 per cent and 7) per cent, namely, a difference of 2) per cent, not only has the old British preference been maintained in its integrity in relation to Great Britain, but the fact is that in some instances we have made the British preference as much as 50 per cent by the addition of an ad valorem duty to a specific duty. Take the case of cement, if you will assume that in Great Britain a barrel of cement costs 60 cents; in the United States, 80 cents. The duty is 7 cents per 100 pounds or 24) cents per barrel if it comes from England, and 10 cents per 100 pounds or 35 cents per berrel if it comes from the United States. What will happen? There is an ad valorem duty of 5 per cent, if the barrel comes from England. That makes 3 cents. 24) and 3 make 27). If the barrel comes from the United States, the ad valorum duty is 7) per cent. 7) per cent on 80 cents makes 6 cents. 6 and 35 make 41. Therefore, the British preference is 41 minus 27) or 13) cents a barrel. Before this tariff was put on, the British preference was 10) cents per barrel. There it is in black and white. So it runs through all that long list of goods that are now upon the free list. You cannot get away from it. You have in one instance your specific duty fixed at so much per article. Then you have your ad valorem duty based on the value. Just as the cost of the goods in England may be less than the cost of the same goods made in any other country, so the British preference is enhanced not by the difference between 5 per cent and 7) per cent, but by the difference between 5 per cent on the cost in England and 7) per cent on the cost in any other country. So the British preference is not only maintained in its integrity, but increased.
I will give a concrete example, in my own experience. When I was in England, a few years ago, the great chief of the tin-plate industry spoke to me of the question of duty upon his product. He said: "I am now a confirmed and convinced protectionist. I am the head of the tin-plate industry. I saw the time when all the tin-plate that went to the United States came from Wales, and my people sent it to the United States; but the United States put a high duty upon tin-plate and developed that industry to such an extent that they supplied every one of their own requirements and also the expanding necessities of the great Dominion of Canada, and we are now shut out of that country. Cannot you impress upon your Minister of Finance and

your Minister of Trade and Commerce the necessity of giving some preferential treatment to tin-plate." I communicated with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and also,with the Minister of Finance. I was advised that they were unable to do anything; but to-night the tin-plate industry of Great Britain is protected at least by a preference of 2J per cent against the tinplate industry of the United States. That must be so, for, while tin-plate coming in from the United States will pay 7$ per cent duty tin-plate coming from Wales will pay but 5 per cent. Therefore, at least one great industry has been helped as it has never been helped by hon. gentlemen opposite.

That is a favourite allegation of hon. gentlemen opposite, but it has not been borne out by the facts in the cement industry.

Let me tell the hon. member for Calgary that the Minister of Finance has the money; he borrowed it in London; he has it in his inside pocket, and he is not worrying about it. The hon. gentleman .says also that the Prime Minister is lying awake at night. What is he worrying about ? You have obtained $150,000,000 from England to pay your bills; why should you worry? What hon. gentlemen are worrying about is how many of their party followers can get a portion of that money; that is their chief source of concern. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia, if all stories are true, has been worrying a great deal. What about the committee which was appointed to look after the money that came from England to be used for the purchase of war supplies when he was on the other side? Has that committee reported to the Government or to the House? Hon. gentlemen are worrying, are they? The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, so far as the question of obtaining money for t'he war is concerned, have never lost five minutes' sleep. They may look solemn and wear a portentous air-as both of them can do with the greatest possible ease-but that is all there is to it. When hon. gentlemen venture to criticise the Government, the Prime Minister becomes virtuously indignant. The hon. member for St. John City, he says, has no business to inquire about submarines. It is true that Walter Long criticised the British Government in respect to the purchase of horses in Canada, but we must not mention submarines. Keep your unholy hands, he says, off this question; do not venture to criticise or make suggestions, even if the national interest is at stake. That is the attitude of (hon. gentlemen opposite. They cloud themselves in an imaginary cloak of secrecy, and tell us, who are the representatives of the free people of this country just as they are, that although these are very serious matters, we must not know anything about them. For Heaven's sake, they say, do not say a word or we will have a general election, and then there will be an awful row.
I intend to discuss this Budget, because I think it is in the interest of the people of Canada that it should be discussed. I do not think that this Budget is a war budget at all. The Minister of Trade and Comrevise:
merce said yesterday afternoon that after listening to the Minister of Finance exchanging compliments with the hon. member for Red Deer upon their being the only two economists in the House, he had an inclination to say to them, " A plague on both your houses ! let us have a little common sense about this Budget." Whose Budget is this, anyway? Is it the Budget of this Government? The utterances of the gentleman who fills the position of Minister of Finance would indicate that the Government had nothing to do with it. Four hundred and thirty-five times he said that it was his Budget. If we cannot believe the Minister of Finance after such a frequent reiteration, I do not know how many times he should say a thing before, we may believe it. The Conservative press announced that the Finance Minister, after careful deliberation, had come to the conclusion as to what the Budget was going to be, but that he was not going to bring it down for a few days because it was thought that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would have to look over it.
I will venture that he never showed it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday showed that he had never seen the Budget before it came down. In the adroit way which is so characteristic of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, he denounced every line of it while apparently favouring it. What about the assertion of the position of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in regard to extravagance in this country? Why should he have asserted his faith upon that question at the present time except for the purpose of indicating to the country, in his own adroit way, that, so far as he is concerned, the present Finance Minister was too extravagant. Apparently a new Caesar Augustus has appeared in this twentieth century who has sent forth the decree that all of Canada should be taxed. That is the situation-taxed under false pretenses. This measure before the House should not be called a Budget, but should be called an act to provide money from the people of Canada for the Canadian Finance Minister under the pretence of a war tax. My right hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in the colloquoy he had with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), announced to the House with the utmost confidence that there were only two economists in the House, himself and the hon. member for Red Deer.
Two in the country.
He forgot the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Yerville.)

He forgot the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Stewart) probably. By the ordinary definition of the word economist I find in the dictionary that it is one who practises economy. My hon. friend belongs to that class of holy Willies who want to offer up to Heaven daily a prayer:
O wad some power the griftie gie us
To see oursels as ithers see us!
If he had that power, he would find that he is not really an economist of the class to which the hon. member for Red Deer belongs, but is a spendthrift travelling under the guise of an economist. But if they are the only two political economists, what about the Minister of Trade and Commerce? He was a good one once; he was good enough for Sir John A. Macdonald, and should we expect that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce will sit there in ecstatic admiration for this new financial colossus who has come in this twentieth century to deal with all financial problems; and our friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was a good one once, is no good now. The Minister of Finance told us that himself, and consequently it must be so.
I submit that this proposition which my hon. friend is asserting in this resolution to go before the Committee of Ways and Means and which he calls war tax, is not a proposition to get money to pay for the war at all. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance gets quite hot under the collar when anybody says that. Last Wednesday he dared any body to say that this is not war taxation. He says that the man on the street knows it is. It is the man on the street, who never takes the trouble to find out what is going on in this House, that my hon. friend is expecting to deceive upon this question. A child of ten years old, he says, knows all' about it. How much does a child of ten years old know about a war budget? But these are the two classes my hon. friend summoned to his assistance as knowing that this is a war budget. I assert in the presence of the Minister of Finance that this is not a war budget, and I Dropose to prove it by a witness whom even the Minister of Finance will be bound to accept. What is the meaning of a war budget? The idea my hon. friend wants to convey to the country now is that Parlia-
ment should pass certain measures by which the Canadian people should be compelled to pay into the treasury of Canada a certain sum of money which is necessary to defray the expenses of the war. That is what I would call a war budget. I say that of the money which will come out of this taxation which is being imposed upon the Canadian people, not a cent will go towards the war and I dare my hon. friend, using the tragic language of the Minister of Finance, who I understand is to follow me, to show me where the evidence that I submit to him and to this House is not correct and does not prove my assertion. The witness I propose to call to prove the statement which I make that this is not a war budget, that not a dollar that will be collected under it will ever go towards defraying the expenses of the war, is the Minister of Finance himself. My hon. friend in his Budget speech, which he delivered on February 11, said.
My proposals for meeting the situation are as follows:
So far as concerns our special war expenditures which may reach one hundred million dollars I should be disposed, if we had not such heavy and uncontrollable capital expenditure to meet, to recommend that we should pay at least a part of it from current revenue. But it is obvious upon a consideration of the figures which I have submitted that we shall not by any reasonable supplemental taxation measures be able to close the gap between revenue and expenditure much less to pay a portion of the principal of our special war outlay In the circumstanres I have no hesitation in proposing to the House that we shall borrow the full amount. required under this heading.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that the Finance Minister proposes to borrow the $100,000,000 from England, and, so far as the principal of that expenditure is concerned, he does not propose to pay a single cent of it out of current revenue. He went on:
Canadian Governments have always justified public borrowing for capital account on the principle that expenditure upon enterprises, permanent in their nature, enures to the benefit and advantage of future generations who may therefore fairly be asked to pay interest upon the debt contracted in respect of them. If this theory is correct, and so far as I know it has never been seriously challenged, then we need have no reluctance in borrowing to meet the expense of this war, because such borrowing is for the purpose of accomplishing for future generations that which is infinitely more precious than material undertakings, namely, the preservation of our national and individual liberty and the constitutional freedom won by our forefathers during centuries of struggle, enjoyed by us to-day and destined, we believe] to be ours for all time. It is therefore the intention of the Government to negotiate for a

continuance of the arrangement which I have mentioned with the Imperial Government for the purpose of procuring the funds necessary to meet our special war expenditure.
So that my hon. friend is getting the $100,000,000 from England as a loan; and last August he put upon the country certain taxes, both by way of customs and excise, asserting that he wanted, the money for the purpose of paying the expenses of the war. Every dollar he got as a result of that extra taxation has been put into the treasury, and is being used for the ordinary services of the country, and not a dollar of it went for the war. Every cent of the $50,000,000 which has been at the disposal of this Government since last August was borrowed from the English Government. Every cent of the revenue collected went into the treasury, and the $50,000,000 which Parliament has provided to meet the expenses of this war has been furnished by the English Government. Not a cent came out of the treasury of the Dominion of Canada, and it will not come out of it under this Government. Why should the Minister of Finance play upon words? Why should my hon. friend the member for Calgary, in the impassioned address which he made a short time ago, talk about these gentlemen being weighed down with their responsibility, about the sacrifice of the Canadian people and country in regard to this matter when these gentlemen who are sitting on the. treasury benches have that $50,000,000 in their pockets, and not a cent of the money that will be taken from the Canadian people under this tax Bill will ever go to pay the expenses of the war? Only yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce admitted that. He said that the Opposition were perfectly willing to vote $100,000,000 for the war, and to provide the interest on it and the money necessary to the nucleus of a pension fund. There is no question about that. He went on in a half-hearted way to attempt to argue certain matters in regard to home expenditures. He was not like the Minister of Finance who declared here the other night that all the evils he had had to contend with since 1911 had been handed to him by his predecessors.

We have experienced a considerable falling off during the past few months, but this my expectation that these dealings will with the coming of spring be relatively smaller, and my hope is that next fall we may regain the losses of any of the earlier part of the year. I may say with confidence that the revenues of the coming year will provide freely for Consolidated Fund . expenditure and in large measure for all capital and special outlays. So far as the financial stringency is concerned we may consider the worst is over.
This As what this seer, the man who peered into the future, was telling this country in April of last year. With a falling revenue, and with an increasing expenditure, he rushed recklessly on to the situation in which this country found itself when the war was on, with a practically depleted treasury absolutely and solely on account of his lack of foresight and because of the spending of many millions of dollars when the revenue was not coming in. All over this land wherever there was an artisan, wherever there was a wage earner, not when the war came on but before, people were looking for their daily bread.
The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) referred to the town of New Glasgow. If my hon. Mend the Minister of Finance had come with me to my constituency when I was home in June last, before the war was on, I would have taken him to the homes of the steel worker and the coal miner in my county and in the county of Gape Breton, and he would have found there that under his administration, instead of the peace, prosperity and happiness which existed in 1911, he bad brought upon these people this woe which he said was never to come upon them. They were without work and without those ordinary conditions necessary to their lives on account of their failure to get work. I will take him now to the coal mines of Nova Scotia where the conditions are not due to the war at all, but due to the absolute failure from the moment he first occupied the position of Minister of Finance to ever take one step which indicated that he had any appreciation of the industrial situation or the needs of the plain people of this country. My hon. friend absolutely failed to peer into the future.
What steps does my hon. friend say he should have taken ?

If this country had not made the mistake of turning out the pilot who had guided the ship of state along a marvellous way, through storms, past reefs and all difficulties, for fifteen years, all these evils would not have come upon us and Canada would have faced this war with an overflowing treasury. What was this hon. gentleman, who could see hi.s way through, thinking about in April of last year ? We knew about this lack of prosperity in our town. Men from the West knew the 'conditions up there last year. They pleaded with him, and begged him, to give some consideration to their special interests. But he refused. Everything is going to be all right; the crisis is past; no more difficulties! So he drifted on spending more money every day and all the time until December 31 of last year. The consolidated revenue fund expenditures were increasing, the revenues decreasing, and he was bringing Canada into 'such a position that to-day he has to come before Parliament and, under the guise of a war tax, attempt to get money

to make up for his recklessness in dealing with the finances of this country. That is the situation. Take some more of my hon. friend's prophetic visions of last year:
So far as the financial stringency is con-'Cerned, we may consider that the worst is over. From this time forward until the culmination of the next economic cycle, we are, on the experience of the past, justified in looking for [DOT]much more normal monetary conditions.
2 deny that this is a war Budget, and I -want to submit the evidence to people who have given any attention to this matter. I do not mean to submit it to the man on the street who will not look at -it or to a child of ten years of age who would not know if he did look at lit, but any one who studies the financial condition of this country will find that the reason why Canada was in the position in which she found herself last year when war came upon us was because my 'hon. friend was 'drifting, did not see what was coming and *did nothing.
He put off dealing with the tariff; he put off making the scientific examination that he was always going to make. He kept on spending money when he was- not taking in money. The returns showed that. The result was that when war broke out in August, 1914, my hon. friend was caught in a trap. All his predictions had proven false. All his prophetic visions had proved to be untrue. The result is that he stands to-day in this unfortunate position before the Canadian people, that he is asking them, because there is a war on, to let him tax them in order to put into the treasury money that would be there if he had been a good and careful overseer.

In regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific, my hon. friend did not always sing this song of complaint. He got into this financial hole as the result of his bad management, and he was trying to put the blame on some one else. As the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce says:	" He would be a bold

I desire to say, both to those of our own Dominion, and to those in Great Britain, if there be any, who have felt misgivings as to the very large amount of estimated expenditure upon the eastern section of the National Transcontinental and the burden entailed upon the country in consequence, that I think it will be reassuring to know that, great as the cost has been, and will be, a large proportion of that cost for the past, has been and for the future (if conditions continue as I believe may very well be expected), will be liquidated from the surpluses on Consolidated Revenue Account and will not become a charge upon the future. I think we are all glad that we are able to make that statement.
He went on to speak in a general way about provision for public works and transportation. The Grand Trunk Pacific and National Transcontinental had not been completed when my hon. friend and his

friends came into power in 1911. He goes on to say:
The greatest problem we have to-day, in my judgment is the problem of transportation- to give our people access to the markets of the world.... The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, part of the National Transcontinental systems is pushing on to Prince Rupert. In time we shall have the opening of the Panama canal. Questions will arise as to moving the wheat to the West and providing terminal facilities for that traffic. Great capital expenditures will be required to provide facilities both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. We must provide adequate expenditures for all these purposes. And if, as I have said, the money is expended wisely and economically, I believe that any Government of Canada at this stage of the country's development will have the hearty support of the people in making these expenditures.
Did he then wish to blame those nasty Grits for having started the National Transcontinental? He was glorying in it. That is not an isolated statement of my hon. friend. He spoke about that question not later than' last year:
"When we consider, apart altogether from its physical resources and its economic strength as a community, the great public works owned and paid for by the Dominion-its canals, railways, including the Intercolonial and the now almost completed National Transcontinental- it can he affirmed with certainty that the national debt of Canada has been kept within very moderate hounds indeed.
And then my hon. friend goes on to say later on in his speech:
Ou railway policy has resulted from the construction of two vast systems within the past year. Construction upon the main lines Of these systems is nearing completion.
In that regard I was very glad to-night to hear my hon. friend the member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) assert that the West demanded that the National Transcontinental should he extended down to the ports of St. John and Halifax. He could not have heard the Minister of Finance denouncing the proposition of the construction of that railway from Quebec to the maritime provinces. In 1904 an election was run upon that question. When my hon. friend sneers at those two rails of rust that exist to-day from Quebec to those sea-ports, he is speaking with the narrow view of some of those Conservatives who at the time of the proposal to construct the National Transcontinental wanted
to take all the trade of the Northwest down by North Bay and Buffalo to the American ports of New York and Boston.
As regards the Canadian Northern, an hon. gentleman opposite said that those babies had been left on their doorstep. I always thought that the Minister of Finance was a Canadian Northern baby that was left on the doorstep of the Prime Minister of this country. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance in his speech endeavoured to justify the construction of the Canadian Northern railway. Here is what he said in regard to the Canadian Northern railway in 1912:
It is to the interest not only of the province of Ontario, hut of the Dominion of Canada as a whole, west and east, that this line, the Canadian Northern line, should he built without any delay whatsoever.
My hon. friend on his own account gave the Canadian Northern a free gift of $15,000,000 in 1913 against the opposition of hon. gentlemen on this side. He came to Parliament last year and with declining revenue actually gave them an absolute present of $45,000,000 against the opposition of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. $60,000,000 of the Canadian people's money, for the expenditure of which, so far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, no man in Canada except the Minister of Finance was responsible! Yet he states that these things were left in his charge. My hon. friend, after the great assertions which he makes in regard to these matters, claiming to be a seer able to see his way through, should not come round with the cry-baby act, but should say: It is true, I had these things; we all thought they were good; but now I have them, and so on that account I am to blame.
This afternoon we had a very interesting performance with regard to the British preference. The Prime Minister undertook, with a good deal of vigour, to lead the Canadian people to believe that this Government in putting a tax of 5 per cent on our trade with the people of Great Britain was not placing any impediment in the way of that trade. He declared that they were going to have 2i per cent more preference -a new preferential policy! The Minister of Finance (Mr. W. T. White) last Wednesday night, stopped himself suddenly in his speech after asking: Who is the father of this preference any way? I think that he caught himself just in time and that he was going to claim to be the fatheT of it himself. Hansard shows that he stopped there

and changed to another subject. What are the facts with regard to the British preference? Plon. gentlemen opposite have never been very clear about their attitude in regard to it-they talk one way at one time and another way at another time. Just now it would appear that their attempt is to run off with the credit of having conceived the British preference and of now making a new one. But their record in Parliament, including that of the present Prime Minister in 1897, shows that they have been opposed to the measure. In 1897, a proposition was made in this House to give a preference to Great Britain in our market. At that time Great Britain had treaties with other countries on the most favoured nation basis. It was impossible to give a preference to Great Britain without it applying to these other nations also, not on account of any trouble that arose in Canada, but on account of these treaties. The preference went into effect, and ultimately, through the action of the present leader of the Opposition, then Prime Minister, the denouncement of these treaties was secured from Mr. Chamberlain, and so the preference went into effect for Great Britain alone and has so remained ever since. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite have put an extra tax of 5 per cent upon all goods coming from Great Britain. Does that mean an impediment to the trade between Great Britain and Canada? Here are the real results. Up to March, 1914, approximately $130,000,000 of imports came into this country from Great Britain. If those imports were coming in this year they would have to pay an extra tax of 5 per cent, or, on importations of that amount, $6,500,000. This is the penalty for the Canadian people trading with Great Britain. All the rhetoric that the - Prime Minister can summon to his aid will not enable him to get away from that proposition - that every $100 of goods imported hereafter from Great Britain will have to pay $5 into the Canadian customs. Now, the great reasons why we have moved in this question is that we feel that at a time like the present this impediment to our trade with the Mother Country is grossly unfair. Great Britain is loaning us the money to carry on the war, and to-day a great many industries in this country-a hundred industries, I understand-are working upon contracts given by the British Government for the supply of munitions of war and other like articles. Were it not for these contracts there would be destitution in many of the industrial 
centres of this country. I know that in the steel centre in my own county to-day-that great industry which, under Liberal rule, was kept busily employed from January to December-has for its only work the providing of these munitions of war for the British Government. Is it right, or fair, or reasonable, that Canada at this juncture should place this penalty upon every Canadian trading with Great Britain? But the Prime Minister says, with a good deal of casuistry: Admitting that it is true-though he hardly does admit it-that you have to pay this money to trade with Great Britain, if you try to trade with the United States it will cost you 7J per cent instead of 5 per cent. That is a peculiar argument. To-day, the increases in transportation charges and insurance charges far more than make up for this 2J per cent of so-called added preference to Great Britain. The result will be that the trade which we have been doing with Great Britain will be driven to the United States, because they are so much handier, and trade with them is free from the difficulty of high freights and high insurance that stands in the wily of trade with the Mother Country. In the eight months down to November, 1914, the latest returns I have, our trade with Great Britain was only $63,000,000, whereas in the eight months of the previous year it amounted to $93,000,000, a loss of $30,000,000 in our British trade. In the same months the trade with the. United States amounted to $336,000,000. The slogan was at one time raised in this country: "No truck or trade with the Yankees." Yet, strangely enough, under the administration of this Finance Minister, the trade with the United States has almost doubled, while the trade with Great Britain has decreased. And if the Government penalizes that trade by this additional tax of 5 per cent added to the other impediments of war time, it will make that trade practically impossible.
It is growing late, and I do not wish to weary the House. I have only a couple of matters further to which I wish to refer. I submit that the attitude of the Opposition with regard to this matter has been more than justified. I have shown, first, that we have the right, in the national interest, to criticise this Budget; second, by the admission of the Finance Minister himself this is not a war Budget-not a dollar of it will go to pay the principal money of the war; third, by the argument of the Finance Minister himself, he was not justified in the attitude he took last Wednesday in discussing this proposition. In the national interest, therefore, and with

the greatest possible satisfaction, I support the amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the Opposition.
The hon. Minister of Finance referred to my right hon. leader in regard to the discussion on the navy. History has shown us that the renegade, having established himself in his new position, becomes more violent in his assertions than the person who previous occupied the position. It is the zeal of the convert, and is applicable to present-day conditions. The hon. Finance Minister, in discussing this question the other night, went far afield with his Shakespearean suggestions, and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister went a little out of his way this afternoon to read from a German newspaper in dealing with the naval question. If the right hon. Prime Minister had made inquiries, I think he would have found that the information which the German newspapers and the German people have is that my right hon. friend had formed an alliance with the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec; that he had three ministers in his cabinet who were s'worn to oppose anything in the way of naval assistance to the. Mother Country. The information which the German newspaper had was that over 20 gentlemen, who were elected to the Dominion Parliament from the province of Quebec, were absolutely opposed to naval assistance to the Empire, and desired to repeal the only piece of naval legislation on the statute book. Speaking for myself, and for hon. gentlemen who sit on this side of the House, I am sure that when the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government announces to the Government his permanent naval policy, he will be bound to announce as his policy the policy inaugurated by the right hon. leader of the Opposition in 1910.
I am sorry that the Minister of Finance is not here with his Shakespearean scene, because I should like to transfer him to the tropics, and to draw his attention to matters affecting the colony of New Zealand. We have heard a good deal about the splendid feat of the Sydney in sinking the Emden, and how unfortunate it was for Canada that she could not be represented by battleships on the high seas. If it vrere not for the Nationalist opposition at Drummond and Arthabaska and the combination between the Prime Minister and the leaders of the Nationalists in 1911, we would have had Canadian Sydneys to catch the Karlsruhe and the Dresden, just as the Australian Sydney caught the Emden. Then there is the Niobe. Any man in the maritime provinces knows
that if the Niobe had been in commission, if she had had her full complement of men and had been ready to put to sea, she could have got after half-a-dozen German vessels that were skirting the coasts of the maritime provinces. The big German steamer, the Kronprincessin Gecilie, has been moored in Bar Harbour since before war was declared; other German steamers passed in front of Halifax harbour-but the steamer Niobe was tied up in deference to the Nationalist sentiment. It was three or four weeks after war broke out before she got up steam and put out to sea; but from that moment to this she has been doing duty in the north Atlantic, side by side with the Berwick, the Cornwall, and the other ships that came over from England.
I want to present to the Minister of Finance the opinion of the Minister of Marine for New Zealand as to the attitude of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Liberal party in this House in 1913 in respect to naval matters. I think Mr. Fisher is a pretty good witness; he knows what he is talking about just as well as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance does. This is what he said on December 3, 1913, after all our discussion of the matter had been concluded.
I quote from the New Zealand Hansard:
The policy of contribution, to my mind, is objectionable. It has been thoroughly debated in the naval debate which has taken place m the House of Commons in Canada. I hold with the view so ably expressed there, that it is not worthy of this country, nor would it be worthy of any other' portion of the British Empire, that we should ask the people to fight for us and not with us. Sir, I cannot Put it into better language than quote a speech delivered by Sir George Ross in the Senate of the Dominion of Canada. .
He then proceeded to quote the eloquent words of Sir George Ross, with regard to the inadequacy of the naval proposals of that time, which had in view the sending of money instead of men. Then he goes on:
A great fight has been going on in Canada for a year in the House of Commons and Senate, as to whether they are going hack to the old and obsolete method of contribution; because giving ships is equivalent to giving a cash contribution, and nothing else-it is a money contribution to a country that has no need of money. . Australia, moved with national aspirations, has already founded her navy, and no party in Australia is so loyal to that navy as her Labour party.
He proceeds to discuss the whole question, just as we discussed it here, and condemns contribution as being absolutely futile. He goes on:
No person in this country to my knowledge has ever been satisfied with the system in

operation-of contribution without representation, without voice, without any say in the control. I propose to quote a few lines from a speech of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, because I think he is a great Liberal whose reputation is world-wide.
The following remarks of the leader of the Opposition, quoted by the Minister of Marine for New Zealand, are very apt at this time:
Mr. Speaker, it is not money that England wants at this moment. England never was wealthier than she is at the present time; her coffers are overflowing. What she wants is the hearts, the brains and the brawn of her subjects ail over the world.
England is not asking us for money; she is giving us money to carry on our part of the war. As the right lion, leader of the Opposition said, what England wants is the hearts, the brains and the brawn of the Canadian boys who have gone across the water to fight; and if it is right and proper that our sons should go over and fight battles of Great Britain on land, were we not doubly right in 1913 when we said: Do not give Great Britain the money, because she does not need it; let us give her ships and men on the sea just as we are giving them on the land. I have had a fairly long experience in Canadian public life. Having taken part in the debate of 1913, I was never prouder of any attitude that I ever took upon any public question than I was of my attitude upon that question; and I know with an unerring knowledge, not with the knowledge of the Finance Minister, that history will say that that is the policy by which, in the end, these various dominions within the Empire must help the Mother Country upon the sea. Sir, history will weave around the brow of our great leader many crowns in recognition of the many wonderful services which he has given to Canada; but among them all there will be none in appreciation of his great career that will show brighter than the clear vision and the insight which he displayed as to the proper attitude of each of the dominions toward the Mother Country in regard to naval assistance on the sea.
The hon. member from Calgary spoke about the consultation which took place in England between Mr. Asquith and Mr. Lloyd George and certain Opposition leaders. It is well known that Mr. Asquith, the Premier of England, asked Mr. Balfour, a Privy Councillor and one of the well-known Opposition leaders, to confer with him in regard to matters pertaining to the war. It 
is well known and has been announced in the Imperial Parliament that Mr. Lloyd George had equally conferred with Mr. Austen Chamberlain. I could understand the Prime Minister giving as a reason why he did not consult with our leader upon the question of the tariff proposals to be submitted to this Parliament-although I think his reason was a wholly inadequate one, in view of the fact that the leader of the Liberal party in this country is not only a Canadian Privy Councillor but an Imperial Privy Councillor as well-that it was contrary to proper usage to discuss tariff proposals in any way previous to their being announced in the House. My right horn friend the Prime Minister knew very well that the oath which binds him and all other Privy Councillors would have bound the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. I am not complaining about my right hon. friend taking that position; he did not choose to' consult our leader, and that is a matter entirely for him. But I think it was extremely bad taste for the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to give as a reason why the consultation did not take place that there were no Balfours, and no Bonar Laws among the Opposition in Canadian politics. I want to say with full deliberation, and I am sure that decent men on both sides of the House will agree with me, that if the hon. member for Calgary in his public career should ever reach in any measurable degree the high place which the right hon. leader of the Liberal party of the Dominion of Canada holds not only in the eyes of the Canadian people but throughout the world, he -will have attained something to which he has no right ever to aspire.
What are the burdens of our hon. friends opposite of which we have heard so much? Their financial interests are provided for as I have indicated; the men of this country are flocking to the standard just as they flocked to the standard in the olden days. They speak of getting the men to go; but, Sir, the Canadian men have "one of their own will, and, from British Columbia to Nova Scotia, they have shown their devotion and interest in Empire concerns without any dragging or compelling. Therefore we on this side of the House do think that we as representatives of the people have a perfect right to discuss this matter, and we intend to vote upon this question along the line of our discussion and to leave it to the Canadian people after they have thoroughly understood it. Whether the question is submitted to them sooner or

later is a matter entirely for the Prime Minister; he will have to take the full responsibility. In regard to the question of the duty of the Canadian people, we on this side of the House, we the Liberal party of Canada in each of the provinces, stand by the Empire in this war for every dollar and every kind of assistance that that party can give at all times until the war is certainly ended.
I could not help being moved to some degree by the earnestness displayed by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) yesterday. The moderate tone he adopted and the manner in which he referred to the war showed to me that he felt very deeply and keenly the important results which flow from this war. We must not, in the heat of debate, forget that Liberals and Conservatives, forgetting their differences have gone to the historical battle grounds across the ocean; and the casualty lists show that death, with even hand, has laid its toll upon the boys, no matter what their politics were. So we, asserting our right as free men in a free Parliament to discuss that which is in the best interest of the country, say to the Government that, over and above all, on this question of the war Canada is not divided and has no question of taking votes to ascertain where the men who sit upon the left of the Speaker are on this great issue. More than ever in all the long history of Great Britain, we join with her living and mourn with her dead, and we look forward with hope arid confidence that, through all the storm and stress of the trying period of war, the prestige and the vigour that have always carried to honour and success heT arms in the centuries that 'have gone will once more lead to victory, and enable her to trample underfoot the militarism of Germany, and to extend throughout the Empire and the whole world the benefit of those privileges of government and civilization which have been the glory of Great Britain through all the ages that have gone.

He is greatly agitated to-night because he imagines he has been denied or, that someone has attempted to deny him the privilege of criticism, and he says it is an entirely new doctrine that he never heard of before, that there should ever come a time in the history of a country when there should be any restraint at all upon party activities or on party criticism. There is criticism and criticism. For myself, and I speak for every hon. gentleman on this side, for fair, co-operative, collaborative criticism we have no objection whatever; we welcome it; it will be of assistance to us. But I venture to say all of us will agree that there does come a time in this country, as in other countries, when that particular brand of criticism of which my hon. friend is the arch-exponent, that brand of criticism which resorts to every scheme of party trickery, which calls up every old battle cry, which attempts to divide along the old lines over and over again, may well be done away with. And who cannot admire the extreme elasticity of conscience of the hon. gentleman who, through the course of his speech, allowed himself to be animated by party bias and to appeal to party spirit in a manner unprecedented since the war began, then closed the same speech with a blessing on those words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which he appealed to both sides of the House to banish party differences and party strife. But, if it is a new doctrine to the hon. gentleman, that criticism may well be held in abeyance while the war is on, while the nation is engaged in a struggle transcending the purposes of party, it is not altogether a new doctrine to his leader, for that leader was one of the first whom I have heard to announce in Parliament that such was his intention, and that by that he intended to abide. It will be found on .page 8 of Hansard of the last session of the House. The leader of the Opposition announced this as his policy at that time.
If in what has been done or in what remains to be done there may be anything which in our judgment should not be done or should

he differently clone, we raise no question, we take no exception, we offer no criticism, and we shall offer no criticism so long as there is danger at the front.
However, the decision on this matter is with the Opposition. They have chosen to swerve from the position taken by the leader of the Opposition last August. They have chosen to base their right to swerve on the ground that certain newspaper publications have not dealt very gently with them; not because, of any action taken by this party or by this Government in this House. They have based their right on the attacks, as they claim, of the publication here in Ottawa called-I do not know its name because I seldom read it myself-called The Press Bulletin, I am informed, and because of other attacks from the party press. I have read some publications, too, and I find myself very severely criticised by a newspaper published in Brockville under the . aegis, I believe, and perhaps under the ownership of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I was attacked for what I thought was a very innocent performance. I was attacked for making speeches throughout this country, constituting an endeavour on my part to aid the country in the war by encouraging enlistment and adding to the spirit of unanimity on behalf of the cause of Britain. But from the beginning there has been no paper more aggressive in its partisan attacks than that very newspaper published in Brockville by, I believe, the hon. member for South Renfrew-unless it is another paper published in Woodstock by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell); and a paper that closely follows them both up is one published in Montreal, I believe under the editorship of the hon. member for South Renfrew himself. However, enough of that. The decision has lain with the Opposition. They have chosen to descend from the high stand they took in August last, and to come down as gladiators on the party arena; and if they ,do there is nothing for us but, as the leader of the Government has stated, carry the conflict into the field of the enemy.
It has been urged by the last speaker that we are trying to sail under false pretenses because we propose to pass our War Revenue Act and to raise twenty-five or thirty millions of dollars for the purpose of meeting exigencies caused 'by the war. This is no war tax at all; it is only a misnomer to call it so; no war tax in any sense of the word, says the hon. member for

Pictou, and he defies me to meet the colossal argument that he advances in support of his assertion. What was the argument? You cannot have a war tax unless you devote the money to the purposes of war! Let me first call attention to the action of the United States. They have a war tax to-day. The hon. member for Pictou has discreetly escaped from the House. " The wicked flee where no man pursu'eth." All parties in the United States state that it is a war tax. Will anybody deny that? Nobody will deny that. Now, will anybody tell me what money they voted and spent for purposes of war?
Is there not room for a difference of opinion as to whether the tax in the United States may properly be called a war tax?

The hon. gentleman
denies it. He assumes to know more about economics in Great Britain and Canada than we do, and now more in the United States' than their citizens do. It has always been admitted to be a war tax by both parties in Congress.
Still in my opinion it is a misnomer.

I have the speech of the President of the United States, a gentleman we heard eulogized to-night by an hon. gentleman opposite, in which he states it is a war tax, and raised because of the financial exigencies entailed by the war. What are these financial exigencies?- diminution of revenue caused by disturbance in trade, and falling off in the receipts of customs caused by dislocation of world commerce. He anticipated that in the United States for the balance of the year 1914 alone there rvould be a falling off of no less than from $60,000,000 to $100,000,000, and to make that up they impose a tax, which they call a war tax, and which 90,000,000 people in the United States denominate a war tax, notwithstanding the better opinion of the hon. member for Red Deer.

Will my hon. friend allow me? In the first speech I delivered in this House I had the honour of pointing out that in the United States they were faced at that time with the greatest deficit in their history because the argument of protection was falling down. Would an extra direct tax at that time have constituted a war tax?

No, because the receipts did not diminish by reason of the war. No war was on then. " You cannot have a war tax." The ingenuity of the
argument against this position was not confined to the hon. member for Pictou, but the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), the financial expert of the Opposition, advanced another reason why this was not a war tax. You cannot have a war tax, he says, until you pay up the deficit between your revenue and expenditure. So long as you have a difference, a hiatus in your revenue and expenditure, you are taxing to make up that and you are not taxing for war. Does anybody adhere to that position now? Does the hon. member for Red Deer think it is correct?

I still think it is a misnomer.
Mr. MEIGHEN. This, then, cannot
be a war tax in the United States at all, because they have a deficit between revenue and expenditure, and to make that up the war tax 'is imposed! If these hon. gentlemen will not 'accept the opinion of the
90,000,000 people that they recently had a great admiration foT, I will meet them with their own opinions expressed no longer ago than last August. One hon. gentleman after another got up and admitted that by reason of the conditions brought upon us by the war we would have to get extra revenue. Does any hon. gentleman ask me who they were ? I have the authorities here. Was our revenue last August equal to our expenditure ? Not at all. My hon. friend t'he Minister of Finance had just announced that by reason of the conditions that had been brought upon us, our revenue was not equal to our expenditure, and a tax was necessary because the deficiency was even greater by reason of the disturbance in Europe. The argument that they now advance is taken out of their mouths by their own speeches in August last.
But more than that; the hon. member for Halifax, the financial expert, says that it is not a war tax, because there has really been no or little disturbance at all on account of anything. I have his words before me, and I quote them very closely when I say that the effect of his statement was that to no substantial extent had the war affected the revenue of Canada. My hon. friend does not say stronger words can be used; I believe they could, and he is the man who used them. He does not think we have suffered much by reason of the war. His words were these-he uttered them himself-that the conditions that had obtained before resulting in the diminution of our revenue had been " extremely accentuated " by the war, and he agrees with that to-day.
I said so. The word I used on this occasion was " aggravated." I make the admission quite freely.

My hon. friend said that it had been aggravated. Last August he said that the condition had been extremely accentuated by the war. not know just the year when the hon. gentleman came to this country; but I have a tolerably accurate idea, and I make this- statement, that I do not believe that since he landed on Canadian soil he ever saw a Liberal Government pay its way during a single year of its existence, and that he did not see any Government in Canada pay its way, that is, collect during the year as much money as it spent during that year, until the Minister of Finance who now adorns that portfolio took his seat as Minister of Finance.
