We must have our tax. If it is to be a war tax, it must, he says, be on articles relatively cheap and of universal consumption. I see the leader of the Opposition consulting with his friend on his left, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), and I am rather inclined to believe that he thinks that I am not correctly quoting his financial expert.
I was saying that my hon. friend was not speaking to the question.

For any fear that my right hon. friend might later on develop, I will quote exactly what the hon. junior member for Halifax said:
Now what should he the main features of a war revenue tax? It should be made as much as possible on articles relatively cheap and of universal consumption.
In order to show that he was firm in his allegiance to that doctrine, just a few pages afterwards he goes on to criticise this Government because it did not put a tax on tea. He says: It shows that you were not animated by considerations of patriotism at all; you were animated by considerations of politics alone, by unworthy considerations, because you refused to put a tax upon tea. He says: I am the father of this doctrine, and I speak for every member behind me when I say that when you are taxing for the purposes of the war, you must tax things relatively cheap and of universal consumption. Will the right hon. leader of the Oppo-

sition say that luxuries are relatively cheap and of universal consumption? Has he come to the conclusion or has his financial expert that the poor people are not using things of universal consumption, but that they are consuming luxuries? Does he agree with the hon. member for Halifax? I can-nbt get an answer out of him. There is the basic teaching of the Opposition that when you put on a war revenue tax it must be its cardinal and universal principle, so it is propounded by the hon. member for Halifax, whom the right hon. gentleman set up to lead the way for the Opposition in this discussion. No doubt he told the hon. member for Halifax to say that in every line of his speech he spoke for every hon. member of the Opposition.
I set out to say that, if we follow hon. gentlemen opposite, we never can raise a dollar upon anything one way or another. I invite any hon. gentleman opposite to suggest a single tax, not at present in the Budget, that we possibly can impose and at the same time not conflict directly with the dictum of some hon. gentleman on the other side. We could not impose a dollar of taxation and not fly directly in the face of the principles propounded in this House by the hon. member for Halifax speaking for every member of the Opposition. Nor could we save money either and not run directly against the principles preached from end to end in Canada last June and later than that by hon. gentlemen opposite. How then are we to get a war tax? War without taxation is the policy of hon gentlemen opposite. Live on some one else! Do not pay the money! Vote it out of the treasury, if you like, but do not get it from any one! That is the war policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. Adopt the C.O.D. policy of the Liberal party in 1900, and send the soldiers away at the expense of Great Britain.
But we have a suggestion from hon. gentlemen opposite. Perhaps I did not do justice to every hon. member opposite. I do not see it included in the amendment of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, but we have a suggestion on the one hand of a land tax, and on the other of an income tax. The leader of the Opposition knew that it would never do to put those into his amendment. He knew that he would not have a show on earth before the people of this country, and that he could not carry his party with him; and he was afraid that if he suggested it, it would be like his suggested free food policy, a policy only "for

the moment." The hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt) suggests a land tax. He wants, he says, to be easy on the farmer,
I am at a loss to know any method by which a distribution can be made that is fairer or easier for the farmer of Canada than the methods of this Budget. The hon. member for Saltcoats offers a suggestion, and tells us that he has the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, of which we have heard in times gone by, behind him in his proposal. They are good citizens for the most part, and on that account their suggestion is worthy of consideration. The suggestion is a tax on land. I will give you as an example the instance of a farmer in western Canada, and I regret to say not an uncommon instance. He is the owner of a half section of land which is worth, let us say $10,000. He owes this year $7,000 against it; his interest is about $3,000. The proposal of the hon. member for Saltcoats is that we tax that farmer on $10,000 of property and let the fellow with the mortgage for $7,000 go scott free. The farmer whose interest is $3,000 pays on $10,000 and the leisured man who has the mortgages for $7,000 pays nothing ait all. That is not an unfair representation of how that would operate in the western country as well as in all parts of Canada. That tax is also open to the same objection as the right hon. the leader of the Opposition levelled against the duties now under consideration. " Ah," says the leader of the Opposition, " you are taxing British goods after they have escaped the German submarine." But what would he have said if we had taxed the farmer's land and the labourer's land? He would have said: "At this hour, when the possibility of our surviving depends upon production from the soil, and when we should conserve production, you impose a tax on land." He would say: " Because the land of the western farmer has escaped the violence of the Krupp machine, you expose it to the devastation of your murderous Revenue Act." Would that not have been the argument in his mouth?
And if we had levied taxes on income, where should we have been? The tax on income is notoriously a slow one and takes years to develop. Further, it is essentially a tax that belongs to the provinces. And when the hon. member for Saltcoats advocates a tax on income I would suggest a course for him by which he might establish himself in the
good wishes of his own government in that province. Let him go to his friends who are in power in that province and urge upon them to establish a tax on incomes. And let him say that if they levied that tax, they might relieve this Government from some of the obligations we are assuming in the way of advancing seed grain. What is the situation to-day? We have the provinces coming to this Government at this time-and especially the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan where there are Liberal Governments-and saying: We have not money enough to take care of the interests of this province and we would like to supply seed grain for the drouth-striken people; but we have not the money; we ask for your assistance. The municipalities come and say: Our land people are the heaviest taxed and they cannot pay, and our land is going to tax-sale. And here would be the remedy of the hon. member for Saltcoats-the only remedy suggested-that while your municipal lands are going for taxes, you should tax them more, and where your provinces cannot get revenue the Government of Canada should invade their field and rob them of what sources of revenue they have.
I have no sympathy in times such as these with a policy of despair. I believe that now, when we are inviting the people of Canada, particularly the employers of Canada from one coast to the other, to stand by their workers and employees, is the time when the Dominion Government should set an example in that respect and not follow a policy of despair. I believe that when we are asking our railroads to struggle against great difficulties and if possible keep every man in their employ, we should not do as suggested by the hon. member for Assin-iboia, weakly allow our railroads to go into liquidation on a mere technicality which would forbid the Minister of Finance to advance money on bonds guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada itself. I do not believe in a policy of this kind, a policy which will allow the industries of this country to lapse further than they have already lapsed according to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). I do not believe in turning more workmen out on the street and adding to the army of workers who in every country to	a great	extent, and
here to some extent, surge around the doors of Parliament. The hon. member for Assiniboia	(Mr. Turriff)
seemed willing to go to the country on this issue. The hon. member for Pictou tried to

modify that attitude to some extent. But the challenge was thrown out, and it lies there yet. Anxious to go to the country! Anxious to go to the country on a policy of timidity and despair, at this time when of all times we should present a strong front to every form of danger. Anxious to go to the country on a policy of liquidation for our railroads, stagnation for our industries, agitation for our western farmers, and starvation for our workingmen. That is the policy inscribed on the banners of hon. gentlemen opposite. At a time like this, I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite should be too anxious to challenge this Government to go to the country. At a time like this when upon the firmness of the grip between us and the Motherland may depend the safety of both; at a time like this when union and co-operation may mean the life of this country; when all depends on joining hands and presenting the strength of all as the strength of one; at a time like this, when all the resources of our country should be conserved to bring about the best results to our people, and when none should be allowed to go the way of waste-at such an hour, I venture to say, the people of Canada, getting behind the sanctity of the ballot, will never reinstate in oflace the destroyers of naval collaboration and the perpetrators of the Transcontinental railway.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) : Mr. Speaker, I must apologize to the House for taking up even a short time at this hour of the morning. The subject has been debated at great length, though not by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), for he only touched it for about twelve minutes. He dealt with everything else, and carried on a very pleasant conversation with hon. members. As I listened to his wonderful peroration about unity, I wondered if he had delivered that to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) in October last. Now the hon. gentleman cries unity; do not break into unity by an election; and a few months ago the men sitting beside him tried to force an election in this Dominion. He should have delivered this oration to them at that time. Why did he not do it?
I want to make myself absolutely clear. It has been said, and said untruthfully, that I challenged the Government to go to the country. I say " untruthfully " advisedly. My hon. friend said that the hon. member for Pictou is not a good reasoner; he himself is a mighty poor listener if he thought that what I said was a challenge.

Members on the other side of the House have been talking about elections. In answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia they have been saying several things about elections. If, in fact, at any time during the session we attempted to criticise, the big club was held up in a threatening manner. I satd to hon. gentlemen, what we do or win not do will make no difference with the Government; they will go to the country if they want to, and will not if they do not want to. I said if they are going why linger shivering on the brink as they did last fall? Why not go? I issued no challenge; I say now that it would be little less than a crime to involve the country in a general election at this time, in the face of what is now taking place in Europe.
My hon. friend insisted that we on this side of the House should tell him how to raise this revenue. Nearly all hon. gentlemen opposite have shown their lack of confidence in themselves by asking the members of the Opposition to frame up a policy for them. My hon. friend began by speaking of co-operation; we invite co-operative criticism, he said.
After the deed had been done.

There was a time when hon. gentlemen opposite could have had cooperative criticism; there was a time when they could have had more co-operation, perhaps, than they can have now. Every time we say anything now hon. gentlemen opposite interpret it as a want of confidence in the Government. Had the Prime Minister of the Dominion been as big as the Prime Minister of Great Britain, a conference would have been held between the leaders of the parties and something would have resulted to prevent, perhaps, all this criticism. I say advisedly that no conference was offered to the leader of the Opposition and no conference was held. The Prime Minister to-day, very weakly, I thought, said that he had sent a programme to the leader of the Opposition. But that is done every session. That is not a conference; that is the supplying of information to the leader of the Opposition as to what the Government is going to do-it is not asking their advice as to what action the Government should take. That is not the way the Prime Minister of Great Britain went about it. The
2 a.m. Prime Minister of Great Britain had a conference at which the advice of the leader of the Opposition was asked, and, no doubt, received. A con-

ference was also held between Lloyd George and Austen Cfhamberlain. That is the course the British -Government took in the way of co-operation. They appointed Kitchener as first war lord, and both parties united to carry on ithe war to a successful issue. But this Government have kept these matters as close a secret as they would keep a writ of general election. Not until they found that the people did not take kindly to their horizontal increase in the tariff did they suggest that the right hon. leader of the Opposition or any member of the Opposition should be consulted. They have departed from every British precedent in the management of the war so far as the Opposition is concerned. By their actions they have -said:	we do not
want the co-operation of the Opposition, except to vote whatever we tell them to vote. That is not co-operation. The hon. Solicitor General comes too late with his invitation for co-operation. He could have had co-operation with the leader of the Opposition, who is a sworn member of the Privy Council, and that co-operation would probably have resulted in a policy not subject to the criticism which is being made at the present time. The Government was more anxious to have an election last fall than they were to have co-operation with the leader of the Opposition; I am looking at men now who know the truthfulness of what I say. I repeat that some members of the Government-yes, I think I can include all members of the Government-were prepared to go to the country last fall and were more anxious to secure a party verdict when ithe Empire was at war than they were to secure the co-operation of the leader of the Opposi tion.
The hon. Solicitor General said that I am the editor of a paper in Montreal. That is not'true; I am president of the company, but not the editor of the paper. I merely want to correct my horn, friend; he himself takes so much care to correct hon. gentlemen on this side when they are wrong.
I said I understood the hon. gentleman was the editor.

The hon. gentleman's
understanding was wrong; I am simply correcting him. He said also that I was responsible for the opinions of another newspaper. I am not going to discuss these two points further than to say to him that he
thinks the Liberal papers are going to remain silent while a newspaper looked upon as the organ of the Minister of Railways and the publications of an organization in Ottawa said to be under the direct control of the Minister of Public Works malign and misrepresent them, he does not know the Liberal press of the Dominion of Canada. In some of these Conservative papers not for one day was there a cessation of the attacks which were made upon the leader of the Opposition. The people of the country will laugh at the statement of the Solicitor General that he and his Government did not know this.
What statement?
I am not going to repeat it; the hon. gentleman will see it in Hansard.
I did not make it.
The hon. gentleman does not know what the statement is, but he says he did not make it.
How could I know what it is if I did not make it?

My hon. friend denied
having made the statement to which I rereferred before he knew what the statement was.

Because I did not
make it.

I want to discuss this
matter fairly. My hon. friend is very clever and very ingenious in twisting things about; I do not think that any other hon. gentleman opposite-not even the hon. member for Calgary-could do so well in that particular kind of argument. Because of my not having the legal training which he has, my hon. friend will excuse me if I do not see the fine points of some of his criticisms. The hon. gentleman spoke of the revenue from excise in connection with imports. I suppose my hon. friend did not mean to say that, but when he comes to read the proofs of his speech, he will see that he did say it. Or perhaps it will not appear in Hansard, because of my hon. friend's having previously corrected it.
I never do that.

In discussing the duties my hon. friend first referred to a decrease in imports and then said that there was consequently a decrease of excise as well. Of course, there is no connection

whatever between excise and imports, because excise is duty payable upon goods manufactured in Canada for home consumption.
Anticipating what I was going to say, the hon. gentleman insisted that I should deal only with current revenue. He knows the way in which he deals with these things when he gets outside of Parliament and has no one in front of him to challenge his assertions, and he insisted that I should deal with them in the same way. I will oblige my hon. friend, if I can, and give him the benefit of any doubt, if he can find any. He pointed to the year 1911-12 as a year in which there was a slight surplus over current and capital expenditure. Does he not know that the Liberal Government were in power in October of 1911, that the Conservative Government not only took over our Estimates, our plans, our specifications and everything but, as his colleagues said, they only completed what we had undertaken; and if there is any credit to be taken the credit is for the Liberal Government. I regret that the Solicitor General is not quite in the Government; there are lots of things take place in council that perhaps they do not .tell him about. They are so secretive I wonder that he found out anything about this war business at all. Now I come to 1912 and 1913. In this House and in the-Conservative press of 1913 what was the answer to the discussion of the Estimates? Why, these are your own Estimates! The late Government went out in October, 1911; the departments had their estimates prepared for 1912 and 1913 and we were told in the House, when we attemoted to discuss the Estimates, that these were our own Estimates; and still the hon. member wants to take credit for them. The Estimates for 1912-13 were the Estimates of the Liberal party and the year's account show a surplus over both capital and current expenditure.
We did not spend all your Estimates.

My hon. friend was not in a spending department. If my hon. friend takes the expenditure he must take the revenue as well. If we are.charged with the expenditure of 1912-i3 we must be credited with the revenue.
I did not charge you.

He was explaining how they got a surplus over capital and expenditure. But the first year the Government makes up its own estimates there is a deficit of $21,000,000. Take 191314 the first year

for which this Government prepared its own estimates, and they came out with a deficit of $21,000,000, if we do what my hon. friend wanted to do, put capital and current expendtiture together. So much for my hon. friend's flourish of trumpets about the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) supporting a Government that did not pay its way. The hon. member for Red Deer was absolutely right and 'hon. gentlemen seem to forget that the chasm between economy and extravagance is the difference between living within your income and living beyond it; and they started to live beyond their income the very first year they had the complete handling of the finances. He made another pecular argument. He said it does not follow that because we are asking for all this money we propose to spend it. He dilated upon that at great length. That is what we have been arguing on this side of the House. Hon. gentlemen, according to the Solicitor General, are putting money in the estimates which they may not expend and on the basis of asking for money which they do not expend they are imposing taxes on the people of Canada. What I say is that they should only ask for the money they intend to expend and to expend economically, and base the rate of taxation on the money which they really want and not on the maximum of what they could spend.

If the hon. gentleman's argument is correct that the money will not be spent for public works or other purposes, then will not the money be put in the public treasury and be available for the purposes of the war?
My hon. friend is now going to tax the people to get a surplus, but is that good financing when the people of this country are in the position we are in to-day?
That is not even honest.

If it is not intended for the war or public works, it is not even honest to ask for it. The hon. member spoke of the Canadian Northern Railway, gingerly, delicately, touched it on one side and came away, then he as delicately touched it up, on the other side, looked over his handiwork said: I think I have polished off that statue very nicely. He forgets that the late Liberal Administration did not aid the Canadian Northern Railway in the extension of its lines west of the Rocky mountains, and that a large share of the money

required to be got through the guarantee of bonds last year was to provide for the railway started in British Columbia by Sir Richard McBride but which they could not finish without more aid. The Canadian Northern Railway in British Columbia is constructed under a provincial charter, not a Dominion charter, under a contract with Sir Richard McBride, and he is to control the rates and not the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. The Canadian Northern Railway people did come to the late Government asking aid for that line, and I say now that we refused them aid for the line west of the Rocky mountains. They entered into a contract with the British Columbia, Government and every person in Canada knew that the railway could not be built under those conditions. Since this Government came into power they came here and got a distinctive grant of money for that line. I think it is unfair of my hon. friend to blame the late Government for all the Canadian Northern Railway expenditure as far as that part is concerned and that was a large part of the $45,000,000 with which the Liberal Government had nothing to do; it was for a line which they did not encourage. My hon. friend's argument is that if the Government had been a Tory Government instead of a Liberal Government they would not have these obligations to meet in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway. If his words mean anything they mean that. Will he. say that he would not have aided the Canadian Northern Railway in any shape whatever from the beginning?

I never argued on the question of responsibility for the Canadian Northern Railway, hut if the hon. gentleman wants to engage in that discussion with me I am perfectly willing.
Mr. GRAHAM; He argued several times on the Canadian Northern railway.

Not in the sense of responsibility for it.
Mr. GRAHAM; Then he was not arguing at all, and I will drop it because he argued that it was one of the lines covered by the $45,000,000. I think he will find on reading Hansard that he left the impression that we were responsible for the Canadian Northern Railway.
Mr. MEIGHEN; I believe you were, too.

My hon. friend says now I am right. I want to ask him this: Would
he not have aided the Canadian Northern Railway as we did, if this Government had been in power? .
I would have dealt with the Canadian Northern railway the same as any other public work.

My hon. friend has admitted that they would have done it. He talks about us taking refuge in silence, but he takes refuge in worse than silence.
I now come to the Quebec bridge, about which I have a little quarrel with the Minister of Finance. The impression has been sent out to the country that this Government had to pay all the expenses of the Quebec bridge. That is rubbish, absolute rubbish, they did not have to do anything of the kind.

If the Postmaster General was in his seat; but he does not need to be in his seat for every hon. member for Quebec knows that both parties for years put themselves on record as being in favour of the construction of the Quebec bridge. I come now to the Transcontinental, one

If the hon. gentleman would do me the courtesy of saying what I stated, I should not have to interrupt him. I said nothing of the sort. I said that we had no security to compel them to take over the road, and I will abide by that till the last letter. I should like the hon. gentleman to show where we have the isecurity. But if we have not, is it not more honest and better to say so ?
My hon. friend is getting very honest.
You had better get honest.
He said that the Grand Trunk Pacific contract was bleeding at every pore. He practically said that the contract was no good.
Oh, no.

I do not want to discuss it at any great length just now, for the time will come when it will have to be discussed. The Solicitor General practicady said that the Grand Trunk Pacific contract was the weakest contract ever drawn up in any country. If my legal adviser told my adversary such a thing as that, he would lose his position mighty quickly. I say the Solicitor General has done injustice and discredit to himself in this 	. J
House to-night. He has told the Grand Trunk Pacific that we have no case.
The Opposition is not bis client.	.
My hon. friend is about that size. My hon. friend says that the Opposition is not his client. Sir, the people of Canada are his clients.
And I tell the people the truth.	[DOT]

I am glad he admits that he tells the truth. Possibly he knows that in_some cases it needs an admission. f I leave it to the country and to the members of this House if I have exaggerated the position taken by the Solicitor General. If he did that in a private case between two litigants he would soon be out of his job as solicitor for one of them. They would tell him to go over to the other side in whose case he had more confidence. There was no necessity for his going to that length at a moment when he admits inferentially that there is a difference of opinion about taking over the road. He practically told this House that the Government has no case. *
No, he did not.
It could not mean anything else.

I think the ex-Minister of Railways in dealing with this subject should be a little more careful than he has been. I said there was no security, but I never said a word to the effect, or even intimated that we could not compel them to take over the road, or that we could noi get a judgment to that effect. I said the late Government failed to put in security. I do not intend to proclaim a falsehood even to satisfy the hon. member.

I am not going to discuss that any more. Had he only said that, it would have been all right. But that is not all he said, and hiding half of what a man has said is the worst kind of misrepresentation. I charge this Government- and the action of the Solicitor General tonight only substantiates what I am going to say. When this Government came into power, for some reason they started to change the grades on the Transcontinental. They will not say they did not.
I say no.

I say they did. They changed the grades on the road, and they

argued in this House by the hour-the Solicitor General knows that-that the changing of the grades did not interfere with the hauling capacity of the trains. But they admitted changing the grade of the road in many places. It is on record. Any person can see it on Hansard. And the Government argued for days, not that the changes were not made, but that they did not injure the efficiency of the road. What happened then? The president of the Grand Trunk Pacific notified this Government in writing that, if they continued to change the grades and structures as they had been doing, the company would not take over the road. That letter is on Hansard and hon. gentlemen can look it up. I think the words of the president were:
Wo. cannot take over the road,** or it was something just as emphatic. But the Government instead of endeavouring to meet the company, continued to change the grades, and I say that the company hardly received a courteous letter in connection with the matter. These letters are all on record in Hansard. With that staring the Government in the face, would not a Government that was trying to make a success of the Transcontinental have met the company and endeavoured to arrange the difference. But that was not done so far as I ever heard. My hon. friend talks about not taking over the road. The Transcontinental is not finished to-day.
Does the hon. gentleman not recognize that he is committing flagrantly the offence he charged me with?

I certainly am doing
nothing of the kind. I am stating what was put on record but what my hon. friend said to-night was never put on record before. This road is not completed. The present Government, instead of pressing on with the work of the National Transcontinental railway, has proceeded not only to change the grades but to make new plans in Quebec. I am not going to argue the efficiency or inefficiency of those plans. The plans were changed, and any correspondence which I have been able, through returns, to get my hands on, does not indicate that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company has ever yet agreed to these changes. It is clear that the road is not completed according to these changes. Surely this Government is giving the Grand Trunk Pacific every possible excuse for not taking over this line-why? If, as they say, the road is two streaks of rust, whose fault is it? This Government is responsible for that condition. Bet
me point out the real situation. The Grand Trunk, in its stress, was not anxious for the operation of the railway down through New Ontario, or a portion of it, but it was made a part of the contract with the late Government that they must take what may be the lean portion for a few years with the fat portion of the line. That was put into the contract. One of the chief duties of the Government in connection with the National Transcontinental railway was to watch diligently so that no excuse should be given to the company for not taking over the road. One of the greatest difficulties we had with the late Mr. Hays was along that line, and after some weeks we succeeded in getting the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific that they would put in their claims as to differences before the arbitrators within a stated time. Had we not done so these claims would have come in long after the road was completed, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company .would have had reason for not taking over the road. Up to the time the late Administration went out of power the Grand Trunk Pacific had not one excuse for not taking over the road. When this Government came into power they proceeded to give them an excuse. They did not even stop at that. This Government hired two partisans at $100,000 to make out a case for the Grand Trunk Pacific. Without discussing that report, let me say that there never was a more misleading document placed before any Parliament or country. It not only was misleading, but in many instances it waa absolutely and wilfully untrue. What have the Government done for the Grand Trunk Pacific? They have had a report made out by their own commissioners showing that the Grand Trunk Pacific had cost $40,000,000 too much, and the company now hands it back to this Government. The Grand Trunk Pacific does not have to make out a case. This Government, entirely for political purposes, and to give two partisans a job, have made out a brief for the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend the Solicitor General is hedging and pretending that there is something wrong with the contract. He sees what is coming, and he now tries to blame it on the contract. The contract was strong enough, but this Government did not live up to it.
The contract was drawn by the Chief Justice of the Dominion.
Had you not better leave that to the engineer?
My hon. friend, who is an astute lawyer, knows that what I say is correct.
I know it is not.

My hon. friend does not know what I am going to say yet. My hon. friend knows full well the strong evidence that was handed to the Grand Trunk Pacific in the form of the report made by their own commission appointed to investigate the National Transcontinental. The Chief Justice of Canada drew that contract.
And he knew as much about drawing contracts as the Solicitor General does.

Let me proceed along another line. I have dealt with the Quebec Bridge, the Canadian Northern and the National Transcontinental railway. My hon. friend has said that these are legacies.
I have pointed out that they would have had to build them just the same. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) said in reply to me two years ago in this House that he had never heard anybody object to the construction of the National Transcontinental railway, but they objected to the cost. It would only be a question of degree as to the amount anyway, because the head of the Railway Department had admitted that they would have constructed the road themselves.
No.
My hon. friend will find it in Hansard.
Had the hon. gentleman not better produce it?

My hon. friend knows that what I am saying is true. I was discussing the statement that some members of the Government were against this road, and the Minister of Railways and Canals said, and it was absolutely true,that he had never heard of any one being against the building of the Transcontinental railway but that they were against it having cost so mucfh. However, it would only be a matter of degree. Let my hon. friend take the Transcontinental railway, which is the biggest matter that he has had to deal with since he came into power, and take the surpluses for which the Liberal Government were responsible, and if he does that he will probably find that he will have a little balance 
in his favour after all charges have been met.
I was pleased with the way in which my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Geo. Foster) addressed the House. He made one statement that seemed to me to come home to the members of the Government. He intimated that the Government could reduce their expenditure by $30,000,000.
I cannot find it.

My hon. friend cannot find anything he does not want to find. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the Estimates this year for public works amounted to $22,000,000. That was an error; the Estimates are $31,000,000. The estimates are $22,000,000 in one place, and $9,000,000 in another. He was discussing what possibly might be done, and when a member of the Government admits there is a possibility of doing this it must be pretty evident that there is a possibility.
Oh, Oh.
Perhaps my hon. friend does not like the Minister of Trade and Commerce enough to want to help him.
Yes, I do.

The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said this:
Make the greatest diminution you safely can in the expenditure of all other departments, and it will puzzle you to produce an economy of $30,000,000.
Hear, hear.

Do not laugh, like the Solicitor General, before you hear the whole
of the statement:
-and still do your duty hy the public administration and the services of the country. Yet you have a deficit of $30,000,000 to be made up.
He goes on and admits-
Oh, oh.

Yes, he admits that there is a deficit of $60,000,000, and he assumes that there could be $30,000,000 saved, and still argues that there will be $30,000,000 left. Surely the Solicitor General does not require to interject anything at all. I am merely explaining what I take to be the real meaning of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I was-a little surprised by some of the remarks that were made by the right hon.

the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden). The speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce was wonderfully eloquent, as his utterances Always are; but it seemed on behalf of the Government to partake somewhat of the nature of a plea of guilty and to beg for a recommendation to mercy. He said: You ought to sympathize with the Government; they are not altogether responsible; perhaps you on the other side are responsible for the major portion of it. I regret again that the Prime Minister did not, like the Prime Minister of Great Britain take my leader into his confidence, because if he had done so he would have secured not only his sympathy but as well his co-operation.
I come now to a point in reference to the real question. I could deal with some figures as to the expenditure, but I will not detain the House, because that question has been discussed so fully that everyone must understand it. This however must stand out, that this Government proceeded to increase the expenditure by leaps and bounds after it came into power, no matter what the revenue was. That fact has not been denied. The expenditure has been increased from $137,000,000 to $186,000,000 and this year to $190,000,000. I charge, not that we are not at the present time in difficulties and must have money, but that it is not fair to blame that necessity on the war and on the so-called legacies left.
I have dealt with the legacies. Now let me deal with the other situation. Prior to the year 1914, yes, before that, as hon. members know, times in Canada were absolutely bad; the financial situation was stringent; the banks had shut down on speculation. Some of us know that to our cost. Business men could not get the credit that they had before. Business in the great centres of Canada was in a state of depression long before there was any war in Canada. The city of Montreal, of which I know something-and I shall be borne out in my statement by the hon. Minister of Justice-and all the other leading centres were crying out: How long will the hard times continue? What is going to be the result? Had not the Stock Exchange closed down, there would have been many crashing failures in the city of Montreal. The Stock Echange had shut down before war was declared.
No 72

Well, let hon. gentlemen look up the matter.
Mr. MEDER1C MARTIN:	Yes, it was
shut down.

I will ask the hon. member for Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget).
I say the Stock Exchange was closed before war was declared.
Because of the war.

That is not the question. I have not come to the reason. I was stating that fact, which every one knows to be a fact. Hon. gentlemen should not rush in where angels fear to tread, when they know nothing about the question.
Long before there was a war, long before a war was expected either by Great Britain or by Canada, times in Canada were very bad, and business was at a standstill and worse. Men did not know where to turn in order to finance themselves. The answer to that by hon. gentlemen opposite is that that state of depression was worldwide. Let me take that view of it. If it be true that the depression was world-wide, and that every one knew it, what was the duty of the Government of the Dominion of Canada? What would any business man have done? What would any board of directors have done? What would any president of a company have done? They would have begun retrenchment long before war was declared; that is, they would have retrenched in every possible way. This Government did not retrench although long before war was declared revenues were falling very rapidly on account of the financial stringency throughout the world, as outlined by the hon. Minister of Finance. The hon. Minister of Finance when he made his Budget speech last year, said that he saw that the clouds were lifting, and he encouraged the people to believe that they were going to have better times. The business men of Canada did not believe my hon. friend.
Mr. W. T. WHITE They did.

My hon. friend says
that they did. Well, wa have met a different class of business men. I have met independent business men whereas my hon. friend has met partisans. 1 met some men in close touch with business affairs, and none of them could see with the optimistic eye of the Minister of Finance. They did not believe, and I did not believe, that times were going' to improve. I do not



charge the Government with bringing on hard times. I am leaving that point for the moment; but the Government with the knowledge that there were hard times, did not take any steps to meet what was coming on account of those hard times, had there been no war at all. I go further and say that, had there been no war at all, extra taxation would have had to be put on at this session of Parliament or else large borrowings indulged in. Had the revenue continued to fall off in 1914 as it had started to fall off before there was a war, there would have been a deficit on consolidated revenue account; but no provision was made by the Government to meet the exigencies of the case, and it went on spending money and increasing the expenditure on consolidated revenue fund from $127,000,000 to $140,000,000, and this year the Government is again asking for the latter amount. The Minister of Finance declares that, through this tariff, he can raise $120,000,000 for consolidated revenue account. We must bear in mind that a tax was put on in August, which the Minister of Finance estimated would bring in $7,000,000 for the balance of the year. That would mean about $11,000,000 for the fiscal year. If he had not put on that tax, we would have had a deficit of $17,000,000 this year, and in the coining year a deficit of $31,000,000 in current revenue account. This Government was remiss in its duty in not preparing for the rainy day when it saw the clouds approaching before the war broke out.
I now come to the point: Are these war taxes? War taxes have been described tonight, but I will make the short definition -taxes on account of the war-taxes that would not be necessary had there been no war. I say that a portion of those taxes would have been absolutely necessary had there been no war. Consequently, to that extent, they are not war taxes at all. The method of raising those taxes has been discussed, and I do not want to go into that question deeply. I was surprised at my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce arguing at length first to set up free trade and then to demolish it. He put up that straw-man, and then he knocked him down, and I think the Prime Minister did the same thing. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that free trade is not practicable in the Dominion of Canada at the present moment. He argued protection and free trade for a long time, ignoring, ridiculing the idea of direct taxation, for-
IMr. Graham.]
getting all the time that part of the taxes for which he was going to vote were direct taxes. The stamp tax is a direct tax. Why should we raise these taxes? We have started out on the principle of raising a revenue by tariff. Had we started out with direct taxation or with some other method, perhaps it would have been as well or better for us; but under the circumstances, for many years to come we shall have to have a tariff in the Dominion of Canada. If that tariff is properly worked, it will be of a great benefit; it will produce a revenue, and incidentally give protection to the industries of Canada.
Now, we have heard about how our own industries were going to be ruined if the policy of the Opposition were carried into effect. The best answer to that is that during the fifteen years when the right hon. leader of the Opposition was Prime Minister in this country, our manufacturing stablishment grew, increased and multiplied both in wealth and numbers as they never did before. We must have a tariff. I had supposed until I had heard some of the speeches that this was a tariff for war that these were war taxes. But from some of the speeches of the hon. gentlemen of the Opposition, I have been driven to the conclusion that that is not the case at all, but that these are taxes not for the war onjly. The Minister of (Trade and Commerce argued for thirty or forty minutes on the question of protection vs. free trade. The Prime Minister did the same thing. The hon. member for Calgary for a long time argued for protection against free trade, and lauded this new tariff. This would lead one to believe that this is not a temporary tariff, a tariff arranged to serve an emergency, but is intended as a permanent tariff. Why go to the trouble of showing that it is all right as a permanency if it is only intended to raise a war tax? I do not know as to these taxes, but this much must be borne in mind- and I think hon. gentlemen will see the force of what I say without it being necessary for the Solicitor General to ask me to get a law book out of the United States Congressional Library and read it-as long as the tariff is not too high it produces revenue but it may reach a point so high that it will defeat this very object. Now, there must be in all the range of articles affected by this increased tariff some-and such have been called to my attention by men who are interested-that are bearing now as high a rate of duty as they can bear. In such cases this duty of 7J per

cent will not bring an increased revenue, but will cut off the revenue from these goods that we have had before. It strikes me as unbusinesslike to take the whole range of articles and simply add 71 per cent, and think that in that way we are striking the happiest means of raising a revenue. I feel confident, from what I hear from men who are interested in a number of lines of goods, that in some instances we shall cut off revenue instead of increase it. I think the Minister of Finance would have done better had he investigated, if you like, and had selected the articles on which an increase of tax will bring in a revenue, and not run the risk of shutting out some goods altogether. If these were ordinary times, we might go into a discussion of protection, free trade or revenue tariff. But, as the avowed object is to raise a revenue and nothing else, let us aim at that object. These tariff changes are for war purposes and not for protection according to what we are told by the Government. Whatever the object, the result is going to be, I am afraid that many things will be shut out and that the revenue from these will be diminished instead of increased.
As to the war taxes, the Minister of Finance put it as a question in this way: Do you want us to stop sending soldiers to the front?-because if we do not get this vote we cannot send them. How, is that correct? Surely it is not. I believe that if this House did not vote a cent of these increased taxes the soldiers would go to the front just the same. I am not arguing that; but I say that the way the Minister of Finance puts it is not a fair way in which to place it before the country. We are not opposing any votes for sending soldiers to the front or for maintaining them. But it might be just as well to intimate that perhaps the present generation should not be called upon to pay all the expenditure for soldiers going to the front. And they will not be so called upon to pay, because the Minister of Finance shows us that he is borrowing most of the money. We will join in giving the Government all the money they want for carrying on the war and for sending our boys to the front. Why, you could not prevent the Canadian boys going to the front; if you did not give them a dollar they would find some way to go. What I point out is that it is not quite fair to the Opposition to represent to the country that if this tax is not imposed our boys cannot go to the front. That is putting it altogether too strong, because in any case our troops will go to the war, and the Government is borrowing the 721
money for this purpose altogether outside these taxes.
Now, going farther, let us take the stamp tax. Some details have been given me to bring to the attention of the Government, but it is too late at night for me to do that now. I do not approve of all the stamp taxes, though I believe that the principle is all right in this case. The Solicitor General spoke of pensions as though somebody were objecting to paying them. There is not a word in this amendment that can be construed into anything of that kind. Nobody objects to paying interest on the borrowed money, and God knows the people of the Dominion are doing their best publicly and privately to help on the great cause in which we are all interested. If we are borrowing money, we are ready to pay the interest; and we are ready also to provide pensions. That being so, surely it is not unreasonable that we should say to the minister that he ought to be careful about imposing further burdens in taxation for what, in a large part, is 'due to over-expenditure, and not the result of war at all.
I realize how late it is, but there are one or two other things I wish to say. (Our boys at the front are standing a good deal more in fighting for this cause than we are in discussing it.) It has been argued that times in Canada are very bad on account of the war. I would point out that the Prime Minister said that a hundred factories are providing munitions and supplies for Great Britain and the Allies. Had there been no war dozens of factories in Ontario of which I have personal knowledge would have been closed at this moment, I am not speaking at random. I might quote the hon. member for West Toronto (Sir Edmund Osier) a good authority on finance, who, if correctly reported, said recently that he was not of the class who blamed the hard times on the war. Let me point out further that the farmers of Canada have been helped out by the war. Crops were not so good in some parts of Canada as we could have desired; and though, heaven knows, we all deplore the circumstances which affect the markets to-day, the fact remains that the farmers of Canada are better off than if there had been no war. And, as I have said, many industries are engaged in turning out munitions of war and supplies that would have been idle or running on short time had there been no war, and I hope they will be able to help the cause of the Allies and that there will be no lack of munitions for the war; Canada in this way also is doing her share. While we deplore the war, we realize that in

speechtext:
That is just what
we heard from the hon. member for Pictou to-night.

I think my hon. friend
has an inverse ratio in his mind. That is what we heard in 1897. What was the result? As I have said, the result was the introduction of that tariff-call it what you like-which included thd British preference and which marked the dawn of the era of prosperity for Canadian industries.
Hon. gentlemen have argued that the preference isbeing maintained. In other words, they are giving Great Britain only one black eye when they could have given her two black eyes. The fact remains that to the extent of five per cent it will be more difficult to do business with Great Britain after this proposed legislation becomes law than it was before. Let me put it this way to the minister. Great Britain is lending us $150,000,000, the interest on which at 4J per cent is $6,750,000. We import from the Motherland about $133,000,000 worth of goods yearly, the duties on which at 5 per cent would amount to $6,650,000. There is therefore, but a slight difference between the interest we are going to pay the Motherland on the money we are getting from her and the height of the barrier which we are placing against British trade. That is, we say to the Motherland: we want your money and we will pretend to pay your interest, but we will put up a barrier against your trade which will enable us to get the money back from you. At a time when we have as our Allies the great nations of the world-[DOT] Great Britain is not our ally; Great Britain is ourselves-is it a time to take such a course as this? The world is largely controlled by sentiment. Is it a time for the Dominion of Canada, whose men are fighting side by side with the sons of the Mother Country, to put up trade barriers against Great Britain, who is supplying us with

money? The Minister of Finance himself told us that we could not get our money except by the consent of the British Government. At a time when our sons are fighting side by side vvith Tommy Atkins in the trenches, is that a time for the daughter to puit up a trade barrier against the great mother of the household? Even if my hon. friend were right-and 1 do not admit for a moment that he is-are the interests of Canada which might be served by these proposals paramount to the great object lesson that would be given to the world at the present time, if, while compelled to raise taxation against the goods coming from other countries, we should not increase the taxation against Britain, who is bearing so large a part of the burden of the world's war at the present time? The Finance Minister ought to see to it-and this is the gist of the amendment of my right hon. leader-that the tariff against Great Britain be not raised at the present time. I have not consulted with my leader, but I think I am safe in making the proposition that if the Finance Minister will agree not to raise this barrier against trade with Great Britain at the .present time, we will withdraw the amendment. This would get rid of the bogey raised by the Prime Minister to-day with regard to want of confidence in the Government.
There is no difference between us at all as to the necessities of providing for the war. There is no difference between hon. gentlemen on this side and hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House 'in the desire to stand .shoulder to shoulder with the Motherland in this great conflict.
We have beside us some of the greatest nations of the world, and with them we join not as Tories, not as Grits, but as the people of the Dominion of Canada, a part and parcel of the great British Empire; we join with these Allies not to 'stop, not to hesitate, not to falter, either with men or with money, until triumph perches on the banner of the Allies and the world is granted that peace, that liberty of action and that liberty of conscience for which Biitish institutions and British Government have always stood.
